projects.readme:
# GUI Desktop Browser

A Windows-oriented desktop web browser built with Python, PyQt6 and QtWebEngine, with tabbed browsing, automatic video discovery and integrated media downloads.

## Live product showcase

These screenshots were captured from the running Windows application on November 15, 2026.

| Welcome screen | Public HTTPS browsing |
| --- | --- |
| ![Welcome screen with browser controls and download sidebar](docs/images/01-welcome.png) | ![Example Domain open alongside the welcome tab](docs/images/02-browsing.png) |

| Video playback and discovery | Completed download |
| --- | --- |
| ![A playing WebM with its detected source in the sidebar](docs/images/03-discovery.png) | ![The same clip saved with a 100 percent progress bar](docs/images/04-download.png) |

## Features

- Browse in multiple tabs with back, forward, reload and address-bar navigation.
- Enter a URL or search Google from the address bar.
- Discover video sources from page elements every three seconds, with a list of detected media.
- Download a selected video or paste a media/page URL into the download panel.
- Run downloads in background Qt threads and show progress and completion status.
- Download direct media files over HTTP; use Streamlink and yt-dlp for supported page URLs.
- Optionally auto-download detected videos and move playing-video tabs toward the front (checked every five seconds).
- Clear detected videos and completed download entries.
- Access FFmpeg conversion, audio extraction and metadata helper methods in the source.

Support for an individual website, codec or stream depends on the installed dependencies and the site's behavior. DRM-protected media and blob URLs are not supported by the page scanner. FFmpeg helpers are source-level utilities, not a complete editing interface or an automatic conversion guarantee for every download.

## Requirements

- Windows is the intended packaging and installation target. Other operating systems have not been validated for this repository.
- Python 3.11 is the tested runtime. The requirements pin Qt and WebEngine to matching versions.
- Dependencies listed in `requirements.txt`: PyQt6, PyQt6-WebEngine, requests, yt-dlp, streamlink and ffmpeg-python.
- FFmpeg and FFprobe executables on `PATH` for media-processing helpers. The `ffmpeg-python` package alone does not install these executables.
- An internet connection for remote browsing and downloads.

## Run from source

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/GUI-Desktop-Browser.git
cd GUI-Desktop-Browser
py -3.11 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe main.py
```

The app starts on a bundled welcome page. Address-bar search uses Google. No administrator permissions are required for running the source application.

## Usage

1. Enter a website address or search phrase and press Enter or click **Go**.
2. Use **+** to open another tab and the tab close control to close one.
3. Wait for the **Detected Videos** list to populate on a page containing supported video sources.
4. Select an entry and click **Download Selected Video**, or paste a URL into the right-hand input and click **Download**.
5. Monitor **Active Downloads**. Files are written to `%USERPROFILE%\Downloads\BrowserDownloads`.
6. Enable **Auto-download detected videos** only when you want detected media to download automatically.

For streams whose total size is unknown, progress may be approximate. A download can fail even when a media URL is detected, particularly when authentication, expiring URLs or site-specific playback logic is involved. Download only media you have permission to save.

## Architecture

| File | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `main.py` | Main window, navigation, tabs, download panel, background download workers and tab reordering |
| `browser_tab.py` | QtWebEngine view, JavaScript video discovery and media-processing helpers |
| `utils.py` | Logging, filename cleanup and opening folders |
| `requirements.txt` | Python runtime dependencies |
| `simple-browser.spec` | Existing PyInstaller packaging recipe |
| `version_info.txt` | Windows executable version metadata |
| `install.bat` | Installs an already-built executable and creates shortcuts |
| `docs/images/` | Screenshots of the running app |
| `assets/welcome.html` | Bundled welcome page |
| `tests/demo_smoke.py` | Reproducible desktop and download smoke test |

Recognized direct media URLs are streamed with requests. For other URLs, the worker tries Streamlink and then yt-dlp. Browser discovery and download extraction are separate steps; the downloader does not automatically receive the browser's authenticated session.

## Windows packaging

Install PyInstaller separately:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install pyinstaller
```

Build the Windows executable:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m PyInstaller simple-browser.spec
```

The recipe produces `dist/PrivateBrowser.exe`. FFmpeg is supplied separately on PATH if you need media-processing helpers. `install.bat` copies that executable into Program Files and creates desktop and Start Menu shortcuts, so that installation step needs administrator privileges. It does not install Python dependencies or build the app.

No prebuilt executable, FFmpeg distribution or release download is included in this initial repository.

## Local data and privacy

- Downloads are saved in the user's Downloads folder.
- `utils.py` writes diagnostics to `browser.log` in the working directory.
- QtWebEngine enables JavaScript and local storage and uses a browser profile. The project does not explicitly enforce an off-the-record profile or guarantee that history and cookies are erased.
- The source enables autoplay and changes the user-agent string. The current “Private Browser” window title should not be interpreted as a verified privacy or security guarantee.
- There is no documented settings-file interface; configure behavior through the existing UI or source.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Missing PyQt6 or WebEngine imports | Install requirements with the same virtual-environment Python used to launch the app |
| FFmpeg/FFprobe not found | Install the executables and confirm `ffmpeg -version` and `ffprobe -version` work |
| Videos are not detected | Allow a few seconds after playback starts; some pages expose only blob URLs or protected players |
| Site downloads fail | Update yt-dlp and Streamlink in the virtual environment and retry with the original page URL |
| Packaging fails | Install PyInstaller in the same virtual environment as the runtime dependencies |
| Unexpected behavior | Review the local `browser.log`; remove personal URLs before sharing diagnostics |

## Development and verification

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m compileall main.py browser_tab.py utils.py
```

The demo ran on Windows with Python 3.11 and Qt 6.8.2. It opened the bundled welcome page and a public HTTPS site in separate tabs, navigated back and forward, discovered and played an eight-second WebM served over loopback HTTP, and saved it through both the selected-video and manual-URL controls. The saved 685,913-byte files matched the original byte for byte. The test also checked progress, clearing completed downloads, and closing a tab.

Re-run the demo with FFmpeg on PATH (or pass its full executable path). This refreshes the four screenshots:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe tests/demo_smoke.py
```

Third-party extractors, external streaming services, the installer, and broader Windows configurations are outside this smoke test.

Report reproducible bugs and feature requests in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/vams2krish/GUI-Desktop-Browser/issues). Include the Python/Windows versions, dependency versions, reproduction steps and a sanitized error message.

## Project status and licensing

This repository publishes a clean source snapshot of the existing Simple-Browser project under the GUI-Desktop-Browser repository name. Generated binaries, build output, logs, bytecode and downloaded third-party archives are excluded.

No project license file has been supplied. Do not assume an MIT or other open-source license from this repository's public visibility. Dependencies and any separately acquired FFmpeg binaries retain their respective licenses.

projects.readme:
# ImmigrationBot

### Waypoint — a private U.S. immigration workspace

**Organize your next chapter with local AI, a personalized document plan, and a clear application timeline.**

ImmigrationBot is the repository for **Waypoint**, a browser-based immigration preparation assistant powered by locally installed Ollama models. Chat and document retrieval run on your own machine, without uploading your documents to ChatGPT or Claude.

![Waypoint production demo dashboard with synthetic case data](docs/showcase/dashboard.png)

> **Project status:** Working single-user local application. Local chat, document embeddings, checklist progress, PDF export, and timelines are implemented. Case-status and processing-time lookups require a configured provider adapter and credentials. Automatic1111 detection is optional; it is not the chat engine.

## Product showcase

These screenshots come from the built app running locally. Case status, processing times, and notice dates shown in the walkthrough are synthetic.

| Personalized document checklist | Application timeline |
| --- | --- |
| ![Checklist with saved passport completion and PDF download](docs/showcase/checklist.png) | ![Timeline with generated dates and a sample notice](docs/showcase/timeline.png) |

| Local knowledge base | Grounded assistant answer |
| --- | --- |
| ![Synthetic guide indexed by local Ollama](docs/showcase/knowledge-base.png) | ![Live Ollama answer citing the imported guide](docs/showcase/assistant.png) |

## Run the production demo

```sh
npm ci
npm run build
npm run demo
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:4327. The launcher creates a separate workspace under `tmp/` and starts a loopback provider with labeled synthetic responses. It never uses your configured case-provider token. Press Ctrl+C to stop it.

1. Choose a visa path and target date. Mark a document ready and download the checklist PDF.
2. Add a sample notice date in Timeline.
3. Enter `ZZZ0000000000` on Overview and request a processing estimate for a demo office.
4. With Ollama running and the default models installed, import [the synthetic reference](docs/demo/waypoint-demo-guide.md) in Knowledge base. In Assistant, enable the knowledge base and ask for the demo review label. The expected answer is **GREEN-LANTERN**, with the imported guide listed as a source.

The November 15, 2026 production build passed 12 automated checks. The browser run verified profile changes, saved document completion, PDF download and content, timeline notices, and case status and processing estimates using the demo provider. Live Ollama passed both plain chat and browser-based document import and retrieval: the assistant returned GREEN-LANTERN and cited the imported guide. Live USCIS/provider credentials were unavailable; the demo does not verify government data. Automatic1111 was offline.

## At a glance

| Capability | What is included |
| --- | --- |
| Private assistant | Local Ollama chat, selectable downloaded models, conversation context, and explicit error states |
| Optional RAG | Import PDF, TXT, or Markdown; local chunking and embeddings; vector retrieval; document/chunk references |
| Case tracker | Receipt validation, provider-backed status requests, saved results, refresh by receipt, and removal |
| Processing times | Form and office filters, provider estimate and source, with no fabricated estimates |
| Personalized checklist | Visa/application path, location, dependents, translation needs, and saved completion status |
| PDF export | Download the current checklist, completed items, timeline, notice dates, and official references |
| Visual timeline | Suggested preparation dates plus separately entered dates from official notices |
| Local integrations | Ollama health/model discovery and optional Automatic1111 API/model detection |
| Interface | Responsive dashboard, keyboard-accessible controls, dialog focus management, and connection settings |

[Quick start](#run) · [Privacy](#local-ai-and-privacy) · [API setup](#case-status-and-processing-time-api-adapter) · [Application paths](#checklists-and-timeline) · [Architecture](#architecture) · [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)

[Download an example checklist PDF](docs/examples/sample-document-checklist.pdf) — generated from a generic H-1B preparation profile, with no applicant data or real case information.


A local React + Express application for private Ollama chat, optional retrieval augmented generation (RAG), personalized preparation checklists, PDF downloads, receipt tracking, and visual timelines.

## Run

Requires Node.js 20.19+ (or 22.12+), npm, Git, and a running local [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) installation. Node.js 22 LTS or newer is a convenient choice.

The default models are `llama3.2:latest` for chat and `nomic-embed-text-v2-moe:latest` for embeddings. Install these through Ollama if they are not already downloaded, or select compatible installed models in Settings. Model weights are not bundled in this repository.

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ImmigrationBot.git
cd ImmigrationBot
npm ci
Copy-Item .env.example .env
npm run dev
```

On macOS/Linux, use `cp .env.example .env` instead of `Copy-Item`.

Open http://127.0.0.1:4317. The server binds to loopback only. No hosting or public deployment is required.

```powershell
npm run build
$env:NODE_ENV = 'production'
npm start
```

`npm test` runs domain and isolated server integration checks. Tests use synthetic providers/models and a temporary data directory; they do not modify the personal workspace. `node tests/live-smoke.mjs` optionally tests real local inference and embeddings, using a clearly marked synthetic document that is removed afterward.

## Local AI and privacy

- Chat defaults to the downloaded `llama3.2:latest` model; retrieval uses `nomic-embed-text-v2-moe:latest`. Change these in Settings.
- Both models must already be downloaded. The app never pulls models or uses a cloud fallback. Remote-backed aliases, even those named `:latest`, are excluded.
- `OLLAMA_URL` must be a loopback host. The default uses `localhost`, which also reaches Ollama's IPv6 listener on Windows.
- Uploaded PDF/TXT/Markdown files are parsed in memory, chunked, and embedded by local Ollama. Text and vectors are stored in `data/workspace.json`; original upload binaries are not retained. Scanned PDFs need OCR before import.
- RAG can be toggled off in Assistant. RAG answers show retrieved document/chunk references; the model is instructed to acknowledge insufficient evidence. Generated responses still require verification.
- Chats are held in browser memory for the current session. Case receipts are sent only to the configured case provider when tracking is requested. Files and chat text are never sent to the case provider.
- `data/` and `.env` are ignored by Git. Protect the local disk and backups: stored data is not encrypted by this app.
- This is a **single-user local implementation**, not an authenticated multi-customer production service. Add authentication, per-user data isolation, encryption, access controls and deployment review before operating for multiple customers.

## Automatic1111

Settings detects the local Automatic1111 API and installed image models at `AUTOMATIC1111_URL` (default port 7860). It was not running during setup. If you want detection, start your existing installation with its API enabled (`--api`). Automatic1111 is an image engine; immigration chat and retrieval use Ollama. No image generation is needed for the requested workflow.

## Case status and processing-time API adapter

No provider key was supplied. The app does **not** invent live results. It displays a clear connection message until configured. Configure a third-party provider or a server-side adapter for your provider's contract in `.env`, then restart:

```dotenv
CASE_API_URL=https://your-provider.example/cases/{receipt}
PROCESSING_API_URL=https://your-provider.example/processing-times
CASE_API_KEY=your-provider-token
```

These are examples of the adapter contract, not a claimed real vendor endpoint. Both requests use `Authorization: Bearer <CASE_API_KEY>` when configured. Secrets stay on the server. For a vendor using different authentication or response fields, adapt the `provider()` function and normalization in `server.js` to its documented API.

`GET CASE_API_URL` substitutes the normalized receipt into `{receipt}`. Expected JSON:

```json
{
  "form": "I-129",
  "status": "Case Was Received",
  "description": "Provider-supplied status details",
  "updatedAt": "2026-10-27"
}
```

`form` and `status` are required strings. No live sample is preloaded. Receipt validation requires three letters and ten digits. Saved cases can be refreshed by entering the same receipt again, or removed from the dashboard.

`GET PROCESSING_API_URL` adds `visa`, `form`, and `office` query parameters. Expected JSON:

```json
{
  "estimate": "Provider-supplied current estimate",
  "asOf": "2026-10-27",
  "office": "Requested service center",
  "sourceUrl": "https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/"
}
```

Processing-time lookup is available on the Overview dashboard and in Settings, and is specific to the requested form/office. Estimates do not predict a particular case completion date. Until a provider is configured, the UI links to official USCIS processing times. USCIS's own Case Status API is a separate integration requiring approved access; no USCIS credentials or access are implied here: https://developer.uscis.gov/api/case-status.

## Checklists and timeline

Supported preparation paths:

- H-1B petition preparation, with consular documents added for applicants outside the U.S.
- F-1 consular visa preparation (not an I-539 change-of-status checklist).
- Family-based adjustment of status inside the U.S. (not family consular processing).

Dependents and translation needs add conditional documents. These are general preparation lists, not exhaustive eligibility determinations; category-specific requirements, exemptions and filing windows must be confirmed against current official instructions. Checklists do not calculate fees or determine eligibility.

A user-selected target date generates preparation milestones at -35, -14 and 0 days, and item-specific suggested preparation dates. These are explicitly labeled **planning targets**, not government deadlines. Official notice dates can be entered separately. No USCIS deadline is inferred automatically.

Download PDF uses the same current checklist, completed items, profile, planning milestones and notice dates. It includes clickable official sources. No cloud PDF service is used.

Official reference sources:

- H-1B checklist: https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/forms/m-735.pdf
- Student visa instructions: https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/us-visas/study/student-visa.html
- I-485 instructions: https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/forms/i-485instr.pdf

## Files and configuration

- `server.js`: local HTTP server, integrations, RAG and PDF export
- `domain.js`: document rules, date arithmetic and retrieval helpers
- `src/main.jsx`, `src/style.css`: responsive workspace UI
- `tests/`: domain and server integration tests
- `.env.example`: configuration template
- `data/workspace.json`: private local persistence (created on first save)

If port 4317 is occupied, set `PORT` in `.env`. Keep the server on loopback. Large Ollama models may load slowly on memory-constrained machines; select a smaller downloaded model in Settings.


## Architecture

The application uses a React 19 interface, Vite 7, an Express 5 local server, Ollama's HTTP API, PDFKit for PDF generation, Multer for bounded in-memory uploads, and pdf-parse for text extraction.

```text
Browser on this device
  |
  +-- React dashboard, assistant, checklist, timeline, knowledge base
  |
  +-- Express API (127.0.0.1 only)
        |
        +-- Local Ollama: chat + embedding generation
        +-- Local JSON workspace: profile, vectors, document text, progress, notices, cases
        +-- PDFKit: downloadable checklist PDF
        +-- Optional case/processing provider: receipt and lookup filters only
        +-- Optional Automatic1111: health and model discovery
```

### How local RAG works

1. Import a supported text-based document through Knowledge base.
2. The server extracts text and splits it into overlapping chunks.
3. The selected local embedding model embeds each chunk.
4. Text and vectors are saved in the local workspace file.
5. With Knowledge base enabled, the assistant embeds your question and ranks compatible document chunks by cosine similarity.
6. The highest-ranking chunks are supplied to the selected local chat model as evidence.
7. The answer includes document/chunk reference metadata for inspection.

Changing the embedding model requires reimporting documents so their vectors use the same model. Retrieval references are not a guarantee of factual or legal correctness; review the actual source and current official instructions.

### Configuration reference

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and restart after changing server configuration.

| Variable | Default / purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `PORT` | `4317`; local application port |
| `OLLAMA_URL` | `http://localhost:11434`; must be a loopback host |
| `OLLAMA_MODEL` | `llama3.2:latest`; initial chat model for a new workspace |
| `OLLAMA_EMBED_MODEL` | `nomic-embed-text-v2-moe:latest`; initial embedding model |
| `AUTOMATIC1111_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:7860`; optional image-engine discovery |
| `CASE_API_URL` | Optional adapter URL containing `{receipt}` |
| `PROCESSING_API_URL` | Optional adapter URL accepting form, office, and visa query parameters |
| `CASE_API_KEY` | Optional server-side bearer token used by the provider adapter |
| `APP_TIMEZONE` | `America/Los_Angeles`; date used in PDF exports |
| `DATA_DIR` | Optional private workspace directory; defaults to `data/` |
| `NODE_ENV` | Set to `production` to serve the built `dist/` application |

After a workspace is created, its model choices are saved in the workspace. Change those in Settings; environment defaults do not overwrite saved selections.

### Local HTTP endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/workspace` | Profile, checklist, milestones, saved cases, document metadata |
| GET | `/api/health` | Local AI, installed models, optional image engine, provider configuration |
| PUT | `/api/profile` | Save preparation path and personal planning options |
| PUT | `/api/completed` | Save completed checklist item IDs |
| PUT | `/api/settings` | Select downloaded local chat and embedding models |
| POST | `/api/documents` | Import one PDF/TXT/Markdown file as multipart field `file` |
| DELETE | `/api/documents/:id` | Remove an imported document and its stored chunks/vectors |
| POST | `/api/chat` | Ask a question with optional retrieval and recent conversation context |
| POST | `/api/cases` | Look up and save a provider-backed receipt status |
| DELETE | `/api/cases/:receipt` | Remove a saved case |
| GET | `/api/processing` | Request a provider estimate with `form` and `office` filters |
| POST | `/api/notices` | Add a user-entered notice title and date |
| DELETE | `/api/notices/:id` | Remove a notice date |
| GET | `/api/checklist.pdf` | Download the current preparation checklist |

These endpoints are designed for this single local workspace. They are not a public authenticated service API.

## Validation

```powershell
npm test
npm run build
```

The automated suite covers receipt validation, conditional document rules, calendar-date arithmetic and invalid dates, retrieval scoring/chunking, local-model filtering (including cloud-backed aliases), provider adapters, document import/retrieval/deletion, citations, persistence, PDF signatures, and cross-origin mutation rejection.

projects.name: iris-control-dl
projects.description: Iris Control [DL]: offline gaze control for Windows and Android. Native Windows mouse/keyboard bridge for browsers and desktop apps, Android accessibility controller, MediaPipe, OpenCV, nine-point calibration, blink/dwell gestures, React/Next.js UI and iPhone setup guide.
projects.readme: # Iris Control [DL] **Your eyes, in control.** An experimental, privacy-first eye and face interface for Windows and Android, with a browser practice mode and an iOS exploration starter. ![Iris Control workspace — actual application screenshot](docs/images/workspace.png) Iris turns front-camera face and iris landmarks into a calibrated cursor, dwell selections, deliberate blink gestures, Windows mouse/keyboard input, and Android accessibility actions. A minimal **Next.js / React / shadcn-style UI / Tailwind CSS** workspace runs as a browser practice page and inside the Windows Electron controller. The native Windows bridge sends input across ordinary applications and browser pages on the primary monitor. The palette uses indigo, lavender, slate, and white, with no green accents. **Project type: Deep Learning (DL), within Machine Learning (ML).** MediaPipe's pretrained Face Landmarker performs neural-network inference. Gaze mapping uses classical ridge regression; smoothing and gesture recognition use deterministic algorithms. This is **not a generative AI project**, does not train a new foundation model, and needs no API key. > **Status: experimental implementation, not a clinically validated or production-certified assistive device.** Unit and build checks do not establish real-world gaze accuracy. Physical-device evaluation is required before relying on actions across apps. See [validation](docs/VALIDATION.md) and [limitations](#limitations-and-roadmap). ## What is included | Capability | Android controller | Web demo | iOS starter | |---|---|---|---| | Front-camera face + iris tracking | CameraX + MediaPipe | MediaPipe WASM, local assets | ARKit face tracking | | Screen gaze mapping | Saved 9-point calibration | Saved 9-point calibration | Exploratory projection only | | Cursor and dwell selection | Accessibility overlay + gesture dispatch | Practice tiles and keyboard | App-local cursor | | Double tap / long press | Deliberate double blink / long blink | Not implemented | Not implemented | | Swipes and repeated scroll | Edge dwell in Scroll mode | Practice scroll buttons | Not implemented | | Home / Back / Recents / Notifications / Quick Settings | Gaze-selectable toolbar | Simulated selection feedback | Use system accessibility | | Typing | Dwell taps on an existing system keyboard | Practice keyboard | Use built-in Eye Tracking | | Phone-wide control | Android Accessibility Service | **No** — own page only | **No** — custom app cannot inject system taps | | Fully local inference | Yes; no INTERNET permission | Yes, assets served from same host | Yes | **Downloads and setup:** [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vams2krish/iris-control-dl/releases) · [Android / iPhone installation guide](docs/INSTALLATION.md) · [Windows setup and controls](desktop/README.md). The ordinary browser demo does **not** connect to or remotely operate a phone or Windows. The Windows desktop app is a separate native host for the same UI. There is no account, server database, analytics, image upload, or cloud inference service. ## Getting started **Windows 0.3 accuracy update:** the 0.2.1 retest still found eye tracking jittery/inaccurate. The new build corrects eyelid-dependent eye coordinates and calibration scaling, adds five validation targets that must pass before eye clicks are enabled, and offers a separately labeled **head-pointer alternative**. For the head pointer, start the camera, select Head pointer, center while still, enable actions, then move your head slightly to steer and return to neutral to stop/dwell. [Mode instructions and measured-check thresholds](desktop/README.md#version-03-choose-an-input-that-works-for-you). Actual webcam usability still requires retesting; a passing unit test does not demonstrate accurate eye tracking. ### Windows desktop control across applications Download the Windows portable ZIP from [Releases](https://github.com/vams2krish/iris-control-dl/releases), extract the whole folder, and run `IrisControl.exe`. Start the camera, run **Calibrate full screen**, then explicitly **Enable desktop actions**. After the three-second delay, switch to Chrome, Firefox, Edge or another desktop app. Gaze moves the real mouse cursor; dwell selects the desktop surface. The top gaze toolbar handles pause/resume, scroll, right/double click, drag/drop, on-screen keyboard, Back, next tab and app switching. **Ctrl+Alt+F8** is the emergency stop. The desktop host keeps local inference running while another app has focus. It uses a sandboxed renderer, a narrow sender-checked IPC bridge, and a native helper with a stale-frame watchdog. It requires Windows 10/11 x64 and currently supports only the primary monitor. It cannot inject into UAC/lock screens or higher-integrity applications. [Full Windows installation, build and validation details](desktop/README.md). ### Web setup and demo Requires Node.js 22+ and npm. Installation and asset preparation need internet access; inference does not. ```sh cd web npm ci npm run prepare:vision npm run dev ``` Open `http://localhost:3000`. Click **Start session**, grant camera access, then **Calibrate**. Look steadily at each dot while samples accumulate. Select practice tiles by holding your gaze; look away to rearm the target. Switch to Typing or Scroll mode to try those practice areas. All practice controls also support mouse, touch, and keyboard activation. In an ordinary browser, the camera stops when the tab is hidden, the session is stopped, the camera track ends, or the page unmounts. The Windows desktop host keeps tracking while another application has focus and stops it through Stop session or app exit. Browser-demo calibration coefficients and dwell duration are stored in local storage; remove calibration in Gesture settings. Desktop calibration is session-only. Camera frames are never persisted. A browser visited over a non-localhost origin needs HTTPS for camera access. ```sh npm test npm run typecheck npm run build ``` `next build` produces the static `web/out/` directory. Serve that directory at the origin root using any static server; all WASM and model assets are local. No CDN is used at inference time. This version does not include a service worker, so offline reload from a remote host is not guaranteed; use a local server for disconnected operation. ### Android controller Requires JDK 17, Android SDK platform 36, and an Android 9+ device with a front camera. Android Studio can open `android/` directly. Use a stable mount in **portrait orientation** for this preview. ```sh python tools/prepare.py cd android ./gradlew assembleDebug testDebugUnitTest adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk ``` On Windows, use `gradlew.bat`. If the SDK isn't found, set `ANDROID_HOME` or create an untracked `android/local.properties` with `sdk.dir` pointing to your SDK. If your system drive is full, set `GRADLE_USER_HOME`, `TEMP`, and `TMP` to directories on a drive with free space before building. The Gradle configuration uses one worker and an in-process Kotlin compiler to limit peak memory; builds still require sufficient RAM and swap. Run Android and web builds sequentially on constrained machines. 1. Open Iris Control. Read the camera and accessibility disclosures. 2. Start the camera and grant camera permission. Allow notifications so the persistent Stop control is easy to find. 3. Run nine-point calibration. Each target has a settling interval and collects 24 valid open-eye observations. Calibration replaces the saved profile only after completion. 4. Open Android Accessibility settings and enable **Iris Control**. 5. Return to the app and explicitly **Enable gaze actions**. Every camera start begins with actions paused. 6. Practice on harmless, large targets. Adjust dwell duration and gesture mappings in the app. 7. Stop from the notification or app to release the camera; use the gaze toolbar to pause actions. The foreground camera service must be started from the visible activity. It deliberately uses `START_NOT_STICKY`: process death must not silently restart camera access from the background. This differs from the original sticky-service request to respect camera permission and foreground-service lifecycle restrictions. No boot receiver is installed. ### iOS exploration See [ios/README.md](ios/README.md). The Swift file is a starter to add to an Xcode iOS app; it is not a signed, build-verified Xcode project. For phone-wide eye control, use Apple's built-in **Settings → Accessibility → Eye Tracking** on supported iPhones. ## How it works ```text Front camera (CameraX / browser MediaStream) ↓ latest frame only, bounded inference rate OpenCV exposure measurement (Android) + MediaPipe Face Landmarker ↓ 478 landmarks, iris ratios, eye openness, head-relative offsets Quality gate → nine-point calibrated ridge regression → EMA cursor filter ↓ normalized screen position + confidence heuristic Temporal gesture engine (Android) / practice-target dwell (web) ↓ action + cooldown + fixation rearm Android AccessibilityService / browser practice area ``` The Android camera frame is rotated upright and mirrored consistently before perception. Gaze features combine both iris positions with two nose-to-face offsets to reduce head-motion interference. This is **not a full 3D head-pose solver or inertial sensor fusion**. The quality score is a geometric/exposure heuristic, not the landmarker model's probability or a validated accuracy measure. The fit learns two five-coefficient linear maps from four features plus an intercept. Closed-eye and low-quality samples are excluded during calibration, and near-stationary iris features are rejected. Android accelerometer and gyro measurements veto actions during device motion; this is a stability gate rather than a fused 3D pose estimate. No automatic online recalibration runs on unlabelled gaze: that could silently reinforce incorrect targets. Recalibration is explicit in this version. ## Default controls | Signal | Default action | Accidental-input guard | |---|---|---| | Gaze held within normalized radius 0.045 | Single tap after 1000 ms | Once per fixation; gaze must move to rearm | | Two deliberate blinks, 180–450 ms each | Double tap | Temporal window and 900 ms action cooldown | | Blink held 850–2200 ms | Long press | Fires after reopening; prolonged occlusion rejected | | Gaze at an edge in Scroll mode | Directional swipe | Dwell delay, central dead zone, cooldown | | Top toolbar target | Back / Home / Apps / Alerts / Quick / mode / pause | Consumes selection without a pass-through tap | | Missing/low-quality face | Suspend actions and hide cursor | Clears pending gesture state | Short natural blinks do not trigger actions. Deliberate blink thresholds vary by user; the eye aspect ratio threshold is currently fixed and requires device/user testing. The single blink is intentionally unassigned. Remap dwell, double blink, and long blink in Android settings, or edit [gestures.json](android/app/src/main/assets/gestures.json) for shipped defaults. All `Action` values are supported. Settings persist in app-private preferences. In this version the top toolbar activates via `TAP`; keep dwell mapped to `TAP` for gaze access to that toolbar. A notification Stop control remains available if you choose another mapping. Typing mode uses calibrated coordinate taps on the installed keyboard. It does not read passwords, inspect text fields, implement an IME, or collect typed content. Small keyboard keys may be too demanding for camera-only gaze estimates. The browser's keyboard is a separate practice surface. ## Performance and privacy - CameraX keeps only the latest frame and requests roughly 480×360 input. Device aspect ratios can select another supported resolution. - Single-threaded Android analysis avoids concurrent model calls. Frames are closed in `finally`; native OpenCV and MediaPipe resources close on service shutdown. - Low/Balanced/Fast frame budgets target 10/20/25 inference attempts per second. Actual FPS is device-dependent and **has not been benchmarked**. - Android thermal status at severe or above reduces inference attempts to 5 FPS. Adaptive camera rebind/resolution control and battery-aware policies remain future work. - Face loss suppresses actions. A stale-frame watchdog hides the cursor after 600 ms. - Android has no network permission, backup is disabled, and no face frames are stored. The accessibility service requests gestures but does not retrieve window content. - Browser inference assets are served locally; it does not use camera frames as network payloads. The server still receives ordinary asset requests. No cloud inference or remote assets are required after preparation. - Model files are checksum-verified during preparation and ignored by Git. Model redistribution/licensing must be reviewed separately from this repository's source license. ## Project structure ```text android/ app/src/main/java/dev/iris/control/ camera/ CameraX foreground service, thermal protection perception/ MediaPipe features, OpenCV exposure gate calibration/ Ridge fit and normalized mapping gestures/ Temporal gesture state machine accessibility/ Cursor toolbar, gesture/global-action dispatch ui/ Compose onboarding, settings, calibration Runtime.kt In-process state and local preferences app/src/test/ Gesture and calibration tests app/src/main/assets/gestures.json web/ app/ Next.js app, responsive workspace components/ui/ shadcn-style Radix/CVA button primitive hooks/ Local camera + MediaPipe lifecycle lib/ Gaze features, calibration, validation scripts/ Prepare local WASM and model assets tests/ Calibration and storage-validation tests desktop/ Electron host, native Windows input helper, portable packaging ios/ ARKit app-local exploration starter tools/prepare.py Verified Android model download docs/ Validation, test checklist, source references, images .github/workflows/ Reproducible web and Android checks ``` Modules are organized as Kotlin packages within one Gradle app module so camera, perception, and gesture logic can be swapped without the overhead of a multi-module build. The web demo uses a static export; a cloud backend would add unnecessary exposure and does not enable cross-app control. ## Limitations and roadmap This implementation is a starting point for iterative assistive-technology evaluation, not a finished replacement for tested platform accessibility features. - **Physical validation:** gaze accuracy, blink robustness, latency, 20–25 FPS, battery impact, glasses, diverse faces, camera contention, and OEM service behavior still need broader hardware testing. A Pixel 4a (5G), Android 14, was subsequently used for install/startup checks, with user-confirmed face detection, calibration and cursor visibility. Task-accuracy evaluation remains outstanding. - **Full-phone limits:** Android protected screens, lock screen, secure flows, OEM restrictions, physical navigation changes, and some custom keyboards may reject or misinterpret injected gestures. No root bypass is attempted. - **Orientation:** portrait/stable placement only in this preview. Rotating, moving the phone, or changing posture requires pausing and recalibrating. Automatic rotation/profile handling is planned. - **Calibration:** ridge mapping can produce poor results when features scarcely vary. Add independent validation targets and residual/error scoring before production use. There is no online drift correction yet. - **Vision:** no dedicated ONNX/L2CS gaze estimator, pupil morphological refinement, calibrated uncertainty model, or accelerometer/gyro fusion yet. projects.name: MathBlitz
projects.description: Everyday math practice for sharper number sense: 12 real-world scenario categories, five difficulty levels, hints, progress, and leaderboards. Responsive web UI and native Android client powered by FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, and optional Redis.
projects.readme:
# MathBlitz ### Practical math for everyday decisions MathBlitz turns the numbers behind everyday life into short, interactive challenges: comparing grocery prices, planning savings, understanding interest, measuring a room, checking a utility bill, and making better use of meeting time. A responsive browser interface and a native Android client share one versioned FastAPI backend. Code-defined scenario templates provide randomized practice across **12 real-world categories** and **five difficulty levels**, with server-checked answers, strategy hints, saved progress, and a leaderboard. **No Streamlit. No external AI service or API key required. No frontend build step.** [Quick Start](#quick-start) | [Showcase](#android-showcase) | [Live Test](#live-demo-verification) | [Scenarios](#scenario-library) | [Architecture](#architecture) | [API](#rest-api) | [Android](#android-app) ![MathBlitz welcome screen with practical math scenarios, five difficulty levels, and account access](docs/images/mathblitz-welcome.jpg) *Actual web screenshots captured on October 28, 2026; native Android showcases captured on October 29, 2026. All visible accounts and scores are synthetic demonstration data, not real users or measured learning outcomes.* ## The Problem Everyday decisions often involve useful math hidden inside an ordinary task: - A larger package is not necessarily the better deal after unused portions are considered. - Two successive discounts are not the same as adding their percentages. - A short meeting consumes the combined time of everyone attending. - A monthly payment difference adds up over years, but is not a complete rent-versus-buy analysis. - A recipe, room, or electricity bill requires converting units before calculating a result. MathBlitz focuses on these practical situations rather than disconnected arithmetic worksheets. The aim is to make frequent, approachable number practice useful to people with different interests and confidence levels. It is a practice tool, not a certified cognitive-health intervention or a professional decision engine. ## Who It Is For | Audience | Useful practice | | --- | --- | | Families and younger learners, with adult guidance | Change, sharing, servings, steps, and familiar quantities | | Students and math-puzzle enthusiasts | Ratios, percentages, estimation, and multi-step reasoning | | Professionals and office teams | Person-hours, task allocation, commute costs, and budgets | | Homeowners, renters, and DIY enthusiasts | Space requirements, commissions, property tax, paint, and flooring | | Educators and math professors | Concrete starting points for explaining assumptions and discussing trade-offs | | Older adults and casual daily users | Short, repeatable practice with real-life contexts | The product direction is age-inclusive, but difficulty levels are **not age-calibrated or validated for ages 5-90**. Current tasks are timed and require reading; some contexts remain more suitable for adults. The existing terms specify a minimum self-registration age of 13, and parental-consent controls are not implemented. ## Project Snapshot | Area | Current implementation | | --- | --- | | Browser client | Responsive HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript, and inline SVG icons | | Android client | Native Java client using the same HTTP API | | Backend | FastAPI, versioned REST endpoints, generated OpenAPI schema | | Durable storage | SQLAlchemy models; SQLite by default | | Shared caching | Optional Redis; local in-memory fallback | | Practice content | 12 category generators, five levels, numeric and two-option answers | | Feedback | Hints, correct/incorrect/timeout outcomes, points, accuracy, recent attempts | | Identity | Username/password registration, scrypt hashes, signed expiring bearer tokens | | Verification | Focused pytest domain, API, security, and legacy-compatibility tests | | Status | Local live HTTP and Android portrait/landscape verified; hosted production validation remains | ### Practice Workspace ![MathBlitz shopping challenge with level controls, answer input, hint action, and progress cards](docs/images/mathblitz-practice.jpg) The workspace combines the scenario, level, countdown, answer controls, hints, and recent results. The example above shows an actual buy-two-get-one-free calculation submitted through the API. ### Explore View ![MathBlitz icon-based scenario library covering shopping, finance, housing, office work, and other everyday situations](docs/images/mathblitz-library.jpg) The library provides a separate exploration view beyond the featured categories. Variation labels in the interface are catalog estimates, as explained below. ## Android Showcase These are real captures from the native Java app installed on an Android 16 emulator, connected to a running MathBlitz API. They are not mockups or a browser dressed up as a phone. Demo history was prepared through actual API submissions; the budget answer and score update were also exercised manually through the Android UI. | Welcome | Live Practice | Correct Answer | | --- | --- | --- | | | | | | Scenario Library | Progress And Leaderboard | Connection Settings | | --- | --- | --- | | | | | ### Landscape Layout The same installed client reorganizes all five level controls into one row in landscape, with a wider scenario card. An orientation change was exercised during the live walkthrough; saved sign-in and account progress were restored. ![Actual MathBlitz Android landscape layout with all five levels and a daily-budget scenario](docs/images/android-landscape.jpg)
More Native Workspace And Hint Views | Workspace Overview | Strategy Hint | | --- | --- | | | |
## Live Demo Verification **Last verified: October 29, 2026.** This is a local production-mode demonstration, not an assertion that a public production deployment has been audited. Uvicorn ran without reload, using an isolated SQLite database, a non-default signing secret, and the in-memory cache adapter. | Boundary | Evidence | | --- | --- | | Automated suite | **24 tests passed**, including real HTTP process tests | | Category/level coverage | All **60 combinations** issued and submitted over HTTP: 12 categories x five levels | | Persistence | Preferences and scores remained correct after stopping and restarting the real server | | Submission integrity | Eight competing submissions produced one `201` and seven `409` responses | | Account isolation | Another account's task submission was rejected with `404` | | Cache refresh | Leaderboard limits 1, 5, 10, and 100 refreshed after a submission | | Android-to-API flow | Sign-in, catalog, preferences, task issue, timeout, correct submission, feedback, and score refresh exercised | | Independent live example | ($279 - $5) / 14 = **$19.57/day**; persisted as correct with **14 points** | | Native layouts | Phone portrait and landscape, library, hints, progress/rankings, and settings inspected | | APK | Built, signature-verified, installed, and launched; signing key preserved across a second build | The web screenshots above remain the previously verified October 28 captures. A new browser walkthrough was blocked on October 29 because local browser access was disabled in the test host's Work settings. Redis/PostgreSQL, hosted HTTPS, physical phones, tablet-specific layouts, and production capacity were **not** verified in this run. See the [full live demo verification report](docs/DEMO_VERIFICATION.md) for commands, evidence, fixes, and release limitations. ## Scenario Library | Category | Scenario families | Skills | API activity ID | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Shopping Value | Unit prices, buy-two-get-one-free offers, package quantities and excess servings | Division, comparison, rounding up | `shopping-value` | | Discounts & Change | Cash change, successive discounts, sales tax | Addition, subtraction, percentages | `discounts-change` | | Budget Planner | Daily allowances, savings targets, spending after bills and savings | Division, budgeting, percentages | `budget-planner` | | Interest & Credit | Simple interest, annual compounding, one-month credit balances | Rates, growth, balance calculations | `interest-credit` | | Housing Math | Bedroom proportions, split commissions, rent/mortgage differences, property tax | Proportions, percentages, time horizons | `housing-real-estate` | | Meeting Math | Person-hours, late arrivals, work ratios, shared workloads | Elapsed time, units, allocation | `office-meetings` | | Commute Costs | Fuel spending, parking/transit comparisons, travel time | Rates, distance, recurring costs | `commute-costs` | | Build & Measure | Paint coverage, tiles with waste allowance, simplified bracket counts | Area, units, rounding, margins | `build-measure` | | Health Science | Steps, nutrition-label scaling, sleep duration, rough heart-rate arithmetic | Subtraction, proportions, time | `health-science` | | Recipe Scaling | Ingredients, cost per serving, whole-pan quantities | Ratios, unit cost, rounding up | `recipe-scaling` | | Home Utilities | Electricity cost, water use, bill increases | Energy units, rates, percentages | `home-utilities` | | Quick Estimates | Pizza areas, rough apartment-sampling rules, household water estimates | Geometry, estimation, assumptions | `quick-estimates` | ### Worked Examples These illustrate supported scenario families; generated numbers vary on each task. | Situation | Reasoning | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | 12 oz costs $3.60; 16 oz costs $4.48 | Compare $3.60 / 12 with $4.48 / 16 | Second package: $0.28/oz versus $0.30/oz | | A $40 item has 25% off, then another 10% off | $40 x 0.75 x 0.90 | $27.00, not $26.00 from a single 35% discount | | Keep $10 from a $70 budget lasting seven days | ($70 - $10) / 7 | About $8.57/day | | Six people attend a 45-minute meeting | 6 x 45 / 60 | 4.5 person-hours | | A 10 ft by 14 ft room needs 12-inch square tiles and 10% extra | 140 x 1.10; round up | 154 tiles | | An appliance draws 1,000 W for four hours at $0.20/kWh | (1,000 / 1,000) x 4 x $0.20 | $0.80 | ### Randomized And Choreographed Content Each generator selects from code-defined scenario families, varies quantities and rates, computes an expected answer, and supplies an approach hint. Difficulty can change number ranges, available branches, or calculation steps. Here, **choreographed** means deliberately structured templates. It does **not** mean a personalized learning sequence, adaptive curriculum, or AI-generated narrative. The original content goal is roughly 10,000 variations per category across five levels. The catalog declares estimates of 100,000-130,000 variations per category. These are **metadata estimates, not an enumerated or exhaustively audited puzzle bank**. Tests check generation and declared estimates, not uniqueness of 10,000 prompts per category. Repeated scenarios, equivalent calculations, and ties can occur. Deduplication and a full content-quality audit remain roadmap items. Generators accept an injected `random.Random` instance for reproducible tests. The public task API does not expose a seed parameter. ## Difficulty And Scoring | Level | Server time limit | Multiplier | Base points when correct | Intended progression | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Very Easy | 90 seconds | 1x | 10 | Friendly numbers and introductory reasoning | | Easy | 60 seconds | 2x | 20 | Short calculations with common values | | Medium | 45 seconds | 3x | 30 | Everyday multi-step reasoning | | Hard | 30 seconds | 4x | 40 | Larger numbers and less obvious operations | | Extreme Hard | 20 seconds | 5x | 50 | Faster multi-step calculation | ```text correct-answer points = (10 x level multiplier) + floor(max(0, time limit - elapsed seconds) / 5) incorrect or timed-out answer = 0 points ``` The backend owns the deadline and scoring; changing a browser countdown does not extend task expiration. Currency and decimal answers allow an absolute difference of up to `0.01`; integer and choice answers require an exact match. Many non-currency generator outputs are rounded to one decimal place. Progress includes total attempts, score, accuracy, average response time, a recent correct-answer streak, and correct answers today. The daily goal is 12 correct answers. Daily aggregation uses UTC. The streak counts consecutive correct results within the latest 40 attempts; it is not a consecutive-calendar-day streak. ## The End-to-End Flow 1. **Open the app.** FastAPI serves the browser client and assets; Android connects to the same backend separately. 2. **Register or sign in.** The API validates credentials, hashes new passwords with scrypt, and returns an expiring signed bearer token. 3. **Choose a category and level.** The client loads the public catalog and the user's saved preferences. 4. **Request a scenario.** A generator creates a task; the service stores a user-owned session containing its answer and expiration. 5. **Solve the problem.** The client displays the prompt, answer controls, countdown, and optional hint. The issue response does not include the answer. 6. **Submit once.** The server checks ownership, prior submission, deadline, and answer policy, then records the outcome. A database uniqueness constraint also prevents duplicate attempts. 7. **Receive feedback.** The response includes the correct answer, result status, points, and elapsed duration. 8. **Review progress.** Dashboard and leaderboard queries aggregate durable attempts, using short-lived caches for repeat reads. 9. **Return later.** History and preferences remain in the database. Browser tokens use session storage; Android maintains local client settings. ## Architecture MathBlitz is a **layered modular monolith**, not a collection of microservices. It separates presentation, HTTP transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence while keeping local deployment small. ```text Responsive web client Native Android client | | +--------- HTTP /api/v1 ----------+ | FastAPI routes and validation | Authentication / practice / preference services | | Domain strategies Repositories and cache port | | SQLAlchemy DB Redis or memory ``` | Boundary | Responsibility | Main location | | --- | --- | --- | | Presentation | Screens, icons, form state, countdown rendering, API calls | `frontend/`, `android/` | | HTTP | Contracts, authentication dependencies, HTTP statuses | `mathblitz/api/`, `mathblitz/schemas.py` | | Application | Register/login, issue/submit task, progress, preferences | `mathblitz/services.py` | | Domai

projects.name: ML-Book-Recommendation-System
projects.description: Interactive Streamlit book recommendation app using item-based collaborative filtering and scikit-learn nearest neighbors. Includes Book-Crossing data, training notebook, saved models, and a detailed README with an app screenshot.
projects.readme:
# Book Recommendation System

Discover your next read through an interactive Streamlit app that recommends books with similar reader-rating patterns. Select a familiar title and explore five related books, with titles, authors, and book-cover thumbnails.

![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11%2B-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)
![Streamlit](https://img.shields.io/badge/UI-Streamlit-FF4B4B?logo=streamlit&logoColor=white)
![scikit-learn](https://img.shields.io/badge/ML-scikit--learn-F7931E?logo=scikitlearn&logoColor=white)

**[Try the live demo on Vercel](https://ml-book-recommendation-system.vercel.app)**

## Product screenshots

These seven screenshots were captured from the live Vercel demo. **Next Chapter** shows real book covers in horizontal shelves. Search for a title, explore five recommendations, and open **Why this book?** to see how the model found each match.

![Next Chapter landing screen with book search and a featured cover shelf](docs/images/01-discover.png)

| Search for a book | Get a reading list |
| --- | --- |
| ![Searching for 1984](docs/images/03-search.png) | ![Five recommendations based on 1984](docs/images/04-recommendations.png) |

| Try another title | Mobile layout | Invalid title |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ![Recommendations for The Da Vinci Code](docs/images/05-another-book.png) | ![Reading list at mobile width](docs/images/06-mobile.png) | ![Prompt to choose a title from the catalog](docs/images/02-empty-selection.png) |

![Why this book explanation open beneath a recommendation](docs/images/07-why-this-book.png)

## Overview

This project implements item-based collaborative filtering on Book-Crossing reader ratings. Each book is represented by its ratings across readers, and a nearest-neighbor model retrieves books with nearby rating vectors. The application uses a selected book as its starting point; it does not require an account or a personal reading history.

The repository includes the data exploration and training notebook, source datasets, saved model artifacts, and an interactive web application.

## Features

- Search or select a title from the trained catalog of **742 books**.
- Request **five book recommendations** with a single button.
- Browse real book covers, titles, and authors in horizontal shelves that scroll on narrow screens.
- Open **Why this book?** on any recommendation to see how it was matched and how many readers gave both titles an explicit score.
- Run inference locally using the included catalog and ratings artifacts.
- Inspect and reproduce data preparation and training in a Jupyter notebook.

## How recommendations work

1. Load book metadata and ratings from the `BX-*.csv` files using Latin-1 encoding and semicolon delimiters.
2. Keep readers with **more than 200 ratings**.
3. Join ratings to book metadata by ISBN.
4. Keep book titles with **at least 50 rating records** in the filtered, joined data.
5. Remove duplicate reader/title pairs and build a book-by-reader matrix, filling missing ratings with zero.
6. Convert the matrix to a SciPy compressed sparse row matrix and fit scikit-learn's `NearestNeighbors(algorithm="brute")`.
7. At inference, rank the catalog by distance, resolve ties by title, exclude the selected book explicitly, and return up to five alternatives.

The included pivot matrix has **742 rows (books) × 888 columns (readers)**. The model uses scikit-learn's default Minkowski metric with `p=2`, equivalent to Euclidean distance; cosine similarity is not configured.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Book metadata and reader ratings] --> B[Filter and deduplicate]
    B --> C[Book by reader rating matrix]
    C --> D[Nearest-neighbor model]
    E[Selected book] --> D
    D --> F[Five titles and authors]
```

## Technology

| Component | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Python | Application and training code |
| Streamlit | Interactive book selector and recommendation display |
| pandas and NumPy | Data preparation, tables, and array operations |
| SciPy | Sparse representation of the ratings matrix |
| scikit-learn | Brute-force nearest-neighbor retrieval |
| Jupyter, Matplotlib, Seaborn | Notebook exploration and model development |
| pickle | Serialization of the trained model and supporting data |

## Run locally

Use **Python 3.11 or later**. The app fits its nearest-neighbor model from the bundled ratings matrix when the catalog loads and caches it for subsequent searches.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Book-Recommendation-System.git
cd ML-Book-Recommendation-System
python -m venv .venv
```

Activate the virtual environment:

```powershell
# Windows PowerShell
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

```bash
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
```

Install dependencies and launch from the repository root:

```bash
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m streamlit run app.py
```

Open the local URL printed by Streamlit, typically `http://localhost:8501`. Select a book, then click **Find similar books**.

## Repository layout

```text
ML-Book-Recommendation-System/
├── app.py                          # Streamlit search and reading list
├── recommender.py                  # Catalog and nearest-neighbor retrieval
├── styles.css                      # Next Chapter product styling
├── Book Recommender System.ipynb    # Exploration, preprocessing, training, export
├── artifacts/
│   ├── model.pkl                   # Fitted nearest-neighbor estimator
│   ├── books_name.pkl              # Titles available in the selector
│   ├── book_pivot.pkl              # Book-by-reader rating matrix
│   └── final_rating.pkl            # Filtered metadata, ratings, and image URLs
├── dataset/
│   ├── BX-Books.csv                # Book metadata used by the notebook
│   ├── BX-Book-Ratings.csv          # Ratings used by the notebook
│   ├── BX-Users.csv                # Reader data loaded during exploration
│   ├── books.csv                   # Additional copies in the repository
│   ├── ratings.csv
│   └── users.csv
├── docs/images/                    # Product screenshots
├── src/                            # Local package placeholder
├── requirements.txt                # Runtime dependencies
└── setup.py                        # Package metadata
```

## Data and model artifacts

The `BX-*.csv` files contain the Book-Crossing dataset. The notebook uses book titles, authors, publication years, publishers, cover URLs, reader IDs, and ratings. `BX-Users.csv` is explored, but reader demographic fields are not used as model features. The other three CSV files are present but are not referenced by the training notebook.

The dataset and cover images belong to their respective rights holders. Review the original dataset's terms before redistributing or using the data commercially. The project does not establish a separate license for third-party data or artwork.

The app reads the ratings matrix and catalog metadata from `book_pivot.pkl` and `final_rating.pkl`. The notebook also exports an estimator and title index for historical use. Only load pickle files from trusted sources.

## Retrain the model

Install the notebook tools in your activated environment:

```bash
python -m pip install jupyter matplotlib seaborn pandas scipy
python -m jupyter notebook "Book Recommender System.ipynb"
```

Run the notebook cells in order from the repository root. Its export cells overwrite the four files in `artifacts/`. Restart Streamlit after exporting so it loads the regenerated files. The `artifacts/` directory is already included in this repository.

## Live demo

The [Vercel demo](https://ml-book-recommendation-system.vercel.app) serves the browser interface in `vercel-demo/`. It uses an exported catalog containing the five nearest matches and shared reader counts for each of the 742 titles. The local Streamlit app computes those matches from the bundled ratings matrix.

After regenerating the model artifacts, run `python export_catalog.py` from the repository root to refresh the browser catalog before redeploying the demo.

## Limitations and future improvements

- Recommendations reflect rating patterns, rather than plot, genre, or semantic similarity.
- Only titles in the filtered training catalog are selectable; new books need retraining.
- Missing ratings and any existing zero ratings are both represented as zero in the matrix.
- Grouping by title can combine different editions or books sharing the same title.
- Cover thumbnails use the [Open Library Covers API](https://openlibrary.org/dev/docs/api/covers). The app chooses the ISBN with the most ratings for each title, so the displayed cover may be from a different edition than the one you read. Missing or unavailable covers show a letter tile.
- The notebook does not report held-out recommendation metrics, so no accuracy or quality score is claimed.
- Dependency locking, automated evaluation, artifact validation, content-based features, and reader-specific recommendations are possible next steps.

## Author and contributions

Maintained by [Vamshi Krishna](https://github.com/vams2krish). Suggestions and contributions are welcome through GitHub issues and pull requests.

## License

There is currently no standalone `LICENSE` file in this repository. Although the original package metadata mentions MIT, explicit licensing terms should be added before treating the project code as MIT-licensed. Third-party dataset and image rights are separate.

projects.description: Educational Boston Housing price prediction with multiple linear regression: 506 samples, 13 features, exploratory notebook, saved scikit-learn model, and interactive Streamlit app. Includes evaluation results, project visualization, setup instructions, and dataset limitations.
projects.readme:
# ML — Boston Housing Price Prediction ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white) ![Framework](https://img.shields.io/badge/App-Streamlit-FF4B4B?logo=streamlit&logoColor=white) ![Model](https://img.shields.io/badge/Model-Linear_Regression-orange) An educational machine learning project that estimates historical Boston-area median home values using **multiple linear regression**. It includes an exploratory Jupyter notebook, a Boston Housing CSV dataset, and an interactive Streamlit scenario builder with 13 inputs. ## Product demo [Open the live Boston Housing Lab demo](https://boston-housing-lab.vercel.app/) The Vercel demo runs the fitted regression in the browser using coefficients exported by `python export_web_model.py`. Submit a scenario to animate the reference and prediction bars and see the dollar contribution of each changed feature. The animation respects your device's reduced-motion setting. ![Production desktop demo showing the animated comparison and feature contribution](docs/images/live-desktop.png) Select **?** beside any input for its definition and an infographic showing its observed range and default. The Charles River input explains both choices. Section help explains the estimate, its comparison bars, and the model metrics. ![Desktop help showing the average rooms definition and range](docs/images/live-field-help.png)
Production mobile demo and field help
### Streamlit screenshots These screenshots come from a live local Streamlit server tested in Microsoft Edge. | Scenario builder | Baseline result | | --- | --- | | ![Desktop scenario builder before submitting](docs/images/demo-overview.png) | ![Baseline estimate of $21,213.23](docs/images/demo-baseline.png) | | Edited scenario | Model notes | | --- | --- | | ![Seven-room scenario estimate of $25,652.06](docs/images/demo-scenario.png) | ![Model metrics, caveats, and notebook chart](docs/images/demo-model-notes.png) |
Mobile prediction flow
The browser test submitted the default scenario, changed average rooms from six to seven, and checked both the new dollar value and the expected change. It also opened the model notes and repeated the default prediction at mobile width. ## Model evaluation chart ![Actual versus predicted home values from the project notebook](docs/images/actual-vs-predicted.png) *Actual output from the committed notebook: test-set values compared with model predictions. The dashed diagonal represents perfect predictions. Values are in thousands of historical US dollars. This is a model visualization, not a screenshot of the app.* ## What the project does - Explores dataset dimensions, types, missing values, and descriptive statistics. - Splits the data into training and test sets with a fixed random seed. - Fits scikit-learn's `LinearRegression` estimator using all 13 predictors. - Evaluates predictions with mean squared error and R². - Visualizes actual versus predicted values and residual errors. - Fits and caches the model from the bundled CSV at startup. Select **Estimate value** to submit a scenario and compare its result with the default. ## Dataset and features `BostonHousing.csv` contains **506 rows**, **13 predictors**, and the target **MEDV**. The notebook's saved inspection reports no missing values. | Feature | Description | | --- | --- | | CRIM | Per-capita crime rate by town | | ZN | Proportion of residential land zoned for lots over 25,000 square feet | | INDUS | Proportion of non-retail business acres per town | | CHAS | Charles River indicator: 1 if the tract borders the river, otherwise 0 | | NOX | Nitric oxide concentration, in parts per 10 million | | RM | Average number of rooms per dwelling | | AGE | Proportion of owner-occupied units built before 1940 | | DIS | Weighted distance to five Boston employment centers | | RAD | Index of accessibility to radial highways | | TAX | Full-value property-tax rate per $10,000 | | PTRATIO | Pupil–teacher ratio by town | | B | Historical race-derived variable: 1000 × (Bk − 0.63)²; Bk is the proportion of Black residents by town | | LSTAT | Percentage classified as lower socioeconomic status in the original dataset terminology | | MEDV | Target: median value of owner-occupied homes, in $1,000s | The feature order above matches the app and training notebook. The app aligns submitted values to the CSV feature names before prediction. ## Model and recorded results The notebook uses an **80/20 train/test split**, `random_state=42`, with **404 training rows** and **102 test rows**. It fits ordinary least squares without a scaling pipeline or hyperparameter search. | Metric | Recorded notebook result | | --- | ---: | | Test mean squared error | 24.2911 (thousand dollars)² | | Test R² | 0.66876 | These are the notebook's saved results, not a newly executed benchmark or cross-validation estimate. The app multiplies the model output by 1,000 to format a dollar amount. These historical values do not represent current market prices. ## Run locally Use Python 3.11 or later, starting from the repository root: ```bash git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Boston-Housing-Price-Prediction.git cd ML-Boston-Housing-Price-Prediction python -m venv .venv ``` Activate the environment: ```powershell # Windows PowerShell .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 ``` ```bash # macOS / Linux source .venv/bin/activate ``` Install and launch: ```bash python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m streamlit run app.py ``` Open the local URL printed by Streamlit, adjust the neighborhood inputs, and select **Estimate value**. The **Model notes** tab explains the training split, test result, and dataset caveats. ### Explore or retrain in Jupyter ```bash python -m pip install notebook python -m notebook ``` Open `House Prediction - Linear Regression.ipynb` and execute cells in order. Its CSV path is relative to the repository root. The notebook writes the fitted estimator to `artifacts/predicted_price.pkl`. The original final cell also writes the estimator into files named `target_test.pkl`, `target_pred.pkl`, and `residuals.pkl`; those names do **not** indicate saved arrays. These files are legacy notebook exports; the app trains from the CSV directly. ## Repository structure ```text . ├── app.py # Streamlit prediction interface ├── BostonHousing.csv # Dataset: predictors and MEDV target ├── House Prediction - Linear Regression.ipynb ├── artifacts/ │ └── predicted_price.pkl # Legacy notebook artifact ├── docs/images/actual-vs-predicted.png # Notebook visualization ├── requirements.txt # Python dependencies ├── setup.py # Local package metadata └── src/ # Local package directory ``` ## Limitations and responsible use This is a historical learning exercise. The dataset includes a race-derived predictor and socioeconomic terminology that encode problematic assumptions. Retaining these variables documents the original implementation; it does not establish that they are appropriate for real housing decisions. The model has one fixed test split, no cross-validation, no uncertainty intervals, and no demonstrated performance on current housing data. Linear regression can produce unrealistic values for unusual inputs, even when each individual input is within its observed range. Use it for studying regression and app integration, not property appraisal, lending, or other consequential decisions. The app trains with the installed scikit-learn version and does not load the legacy pickle. ## Technology Python · pandas · NumPy · scikit-learn · Matplotlib · Jupyter Notebook · Streamlit ## Author and licensing **Vamshi Krishna Adam** — [GitHub](https://github.com/vams2krish) The package metadata declares MIT, but this repository does not currently include a standalone LICENSE file. Dataset redistribution terms should be checked separately before reuse.

projects.name: ML-Customer-Segmentation-Mall
projects.description: Unsupervised machine learning project for mall customer segmentation with K-Means, feature scaling, elbow-method exploration, and Python visualizations. Includes a Jupyter notebook, dataset, project image, setup instructions, and documented limitations.
projects.readme: # Segment Studio · Mall Customer Segmentation [**Open the live Vercel demo →**](https://ml-customer-segmentation-mall.vercel.app) Segment Studio is an **unsupervised machine learning (ML)** project. Its interactive dashboard uses K-Means to explore how 200 sample mall customers group by age, annual income, and spending score. The browser fits the model locally; customer profiles entered into the app are neither stored nor sent to a server. ![Dashboard overview showing the customer scatter plot, segment mix, and modeling infographic](docs/screenshots/01-overview.png) ## Explore the product - **Overview:** see sample averages, compare 2–8 clusters, and isolate any group in the income vs. spending chart. Each diamond marks the displayed coordinates of a fitted centroid; age is the third model feature. - **Segments:** compare each segment’s customer count, sample share, and typical age, income, and spending score in original units. - **Predict:** enter a profile to find the nearest segment in the current fit. The form validates each field before assigning a group. - **Field guide:** select a **?** to see what a label or control means, including its units and relevant ranges. Press **Escape** or select **Got it** to close and return focus to the control. - **Model walkthrough:** follow the four-step infographic from sample data and scaling to grouping and assignment. ## Product screenshots | Desktop workspace | Desktop workspace | | --- | --- | | [Segment focus](docs/screenshots/02-segment-focus.png) ![One segment highlighted](docs/screenshots/02-segment-focus.png) | [Seven-cluster view](docs/screenshots/03-seven-clusters.png) ![Dashboard refit to seven clusters](docs/screenshots/03-seven-clusters.png) | | [Segment profiles](docs/screenshots/04-segment-profiles.png) ![Profile cards](docs/screenshots/04-segment-profiles.png) | [Customer assignment](docs/screenshots/05-customer-assignment.png) ![Profile form and nearest-segment result](docs/screenshots/05-customer-assignment.png) | | [Chart field guide](docs/screenshots/08-chart-field-guide.png) ![Chart help explaining observed ranges](docs/screenshots/08-chart-field-guide.png) | [Prediction field guide](docs/screenshots/10-prediction-field-guide.png) ![Income help explaining units and input limits](docs/screenshots/10-prediction-field-guide.png) | | [Mobile overview](docs/screenshots/06-mobile-overview.png) | [Mobile assignment](docs/screenshots/07-mobile-assignment.png) | | --- | --- | | | | ![Infographic showing input, scale, cluster and match steps](docs/screenshots/09-model-infographic.png) ## Model and dataset The [bundled CSV](archive/Mall_Customers.csv) contains 200 customer rows. The original source and redistribution license are not recorded in the supplied project files. | Field | Observed sample values | Model role | | --- | --- | --- | | Age | 18–70 years | Fit and prediction | | Annual income | $15k–$137k | Fit and prediction | | Spending score | 1–99, on a defined scale of 1–100 | Fit and prediction | | CustomerID | 200 unique identifiers | Record identity only | | Genre | Categorical field in the source CSV | Excluded | The model standardizes the three features, fits K-Means with 20 seeded initializations per candidate fit, and assigns each record to the nearest centroid in standardized space. The dashboard uses descriptive names based on centroid age, income, and spending score. For example, the five-cluster view includes Young high scorers and High-income low scorers. Names can change when the cluster count changes. Five is an exploratory starting point. The notebook also compares inertia and silhouette scores across 2–8 clusters. The browser and scikit-learn use different initializers; exact assignments can differ. This small sample supports exploration. An assignment does not express confidence or validate a business segment, especially for inputs outside the observed ranges. ## Design system The UI uses a **midnight navy** canvas (`#101725`), **slate** panels (`#151F31`), and **lime** accents (`#B5ED78`) for active navigation, focus, and primary actions. Segments use a separate categorical palette carried through plots, bars, profiles, and results. Labels and counts supplement the colors. The workspace switches to stacked cards and compact navigation on mobile. ## Run and test locally Use Node.js 24 or newer for the web app. ```sh npm ci npm run dev npm run build npm test npx playwright install chromium npm run test:e2e ``` Model tests cover all supported cluster counts, centroid means, reproducibility, identifier exclusion, and invalid inputs. Browser tests cover segment filtering, refitting, profiles, prediction and validation, mobile layout, keyboard navigation, field-guide ranges and focus restoration, and the live infographic. To regenerate screenshots, set `CAPTURE_SCREENSHOTS=1` before running the browser tests. Open the [executed Python notebook](Customer-Segmentation-Mall.ipynb) from the repository root: ```sh python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python -m notebook Customer-Segmentation-Mall.ipynb ``` The web app is a static Vite build deployed to Vercel. To update the linked project from an authenticated checkout, run `npx vercel deploy --prod`. GitHub auto-deploy requires a separate GitHub login connection in Vercel. ## Source map - `src/model.js` — CSV validation, scaling, K-Means, and nearest-centroid assignment. - `src/app.js`, `src/help.js`, `src/style.css` — dashboard, field guide, and design tokens. - `tests/` — model and browser checks. - `docs/screenshots/` — real product captures.
