projects.name: ML-FlowRank
projects.description: ML-powered video discovery demo with playable original clips, private PostgreSQL guest sessions, personalized ranking, privacy controls, moderation, experiments, temporal evaluation, and illustrated product showcases.
projects.readme: # ML — FlowRank ↗ **A short-form discovery product with machine learning ranking, 120 playable real-world videos, private guest sessions and a durable feedback loop.** ![FlowRank discovery feed on desktop](docs/screenshots/01-discovery-desktop.png) **Project type: Machine Learning (ML).** FlowRank uses logistic regression for ranking, with personalized retrieval, bounded exploration and diversity reranking. It does not use deep learning or generative AI, and does not reproduce TikTok's proprietary algorithm. [Open the live demo](https://ml-flowrank.vercel.app) ## Product showcase Screenshots from the running app. ### Explore the catalog ![Searchable real-video catalog](docs/screenshots/05-explore-catalog.png) ### Saved reels ![Private saved reels collection](docs/screenshots/06-saved-reels.png) ### Your curiosity, in focus See actual session impressions, feedback and your evolving interest map. ![Personal insights and discovery activity](docs/screenshots/02-personal-insights.png) ### Your feed, your rules Turn personalization off, export your activity or delete the current session and its data. ![Privacy settings, personalization toggle, export and deletion controls](docs/screenshots/03-privacy-controls.png) ### Discovery on mobile The same playable feed adapts to a narrow screen, with topic chips and accessible playback actions. ## What is implemented | Area | Implementation | | --- | --- | | Product | Vertical video player, topic filters, catalog search, private saved reels, like/next/hide actions, keyboard shortcuts, responsive layout, personal insights and privacy dialog | | Media | 120 distinct Wikimedia Commons videos across Travel, Cooking, Technology, Music, Fitness and Art. Each reel links to its author credits and license. | | Identity | Random 256-bit guest bearer cookie; Secure in production, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax; only token hashes stored | | Persistence | PostgreSQL/Supabase in production; request-scoped transactions via Supavisor; SQLite for local development | | Isolation | Private `flowrank` schema, least-privilege runtime login, forced PostgreSQL row-level security on session activity | | Feedback | Measured visible playback fractions, explicit likes/skips/hides, exposure ownership, duplicate prevention and elapsed-time bounds | | Recommendations | Candidate union from affinity/freshness/popularity, learned ranking, stable exploration, topic and creator diversity | | Experiments | Stable 50/50 session assignment to balanced/diverse variants, exposure and model-feature logging | | Privacy | Personalization opt-out, activity export, immediate cascade deletion, 30-day session expiry and protected daily retention job | | Moderation | Pending/approved/blocked states, eligibility filters, session-specific hiding and authenticated admin metadata ingestion | | ML lifecycle | Versioned model artifact, chronological split, log loss, NDCG@10, Recall@10, optional training on explicitly labeled exports | | Operations | Flask WSGI/Vercel Python deployment, Waitress locally, health endpoint, request IDs, structured timings, CSP and rate limits | | Verification | Python unit/API tests, real PostgreSQL RLS test, desktop/mobile browser tests and GitHub Actions | The hosted demo is designed for public product evaluation. It is not a claim of production readiness for a large user-generated video platform: training data and catalog quality/popularity are synthetic, the catalog is small, and sustained load, disaster recovery and independent security audits remain future work. ## Run locally Requires Python 3.10+; the hosted runtime uses Python 3.12. The trained model and real-video manifest are committed, so no API key or training step is required. Real video playback requires internet access to Wikimedia Commons. ```bash git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-FlowRank.git cd ML-FlowRank python -m pip install -r requirements.txt python app.py ``` Open **http://127.0.0.1:8000**. A private guest session starts automatically. Watch a clip, like it, move to the next discovery, then open **Your insights**. Refreshing preserves the session. Privacy controls are available from the guest avatar on all screen sizes. Without `DATABASE_URL`, the application uses `data/product.db` locally. On Vercel, the app requires PostgreSQL and refuses to fall back to ephemeral storage. Environment names and descriptions are in [.env.example](.env.example). Python does not automatically load `.env.local`; supply environment variables through your terminal or hosting environment. The original dependency-free v1 engine remains available through `python -m flowrank.server` and `python -m flowrank.train` for comparison. **Use `python app.py` for the current product.** ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Reviewed video catalog] --> B[Eligible candidate retrieval] C[Private guest session] --> D[Decayed topic interests] D --> B B --> E[Versioned logistic ranker] E --> F[Exploration and diversity] F --> G[Vertical video player] G --> H[Visible impression and playback feedback] H --> I[PostgreSQL with row security] I --> D J[Explicit exports or synthetic examples] --> K[Temporal training and evaluation] K --> E ``` 1. **Start privately.** The server creates an opaque guest session. Requests cannot choose another user's ID. Guests are browser-bound, not email/password accounts. 2. **Filter eligible content.** Only approved videos enter the feed. Reported items stay hidden for that guest; recently watched/skipped items are excluded for 30 minutes. 3. **Build interests.** Likes contribute +1, skips −0.6, hides −2, and watches `2 × fraction − 0.5`. Contributions decay with a seven-day time constant, are limited to the session's retention window and pass through `tanh(total / 3)`. Opting out zeros these features. 4. **Retrieve and rank.** Union up to 40 items each from affinity, freshness and popularity, then rank from four features: affinity, quality, freshness and popularity. This reference implementation scans a small indexed catalog; it does not claim an ANN retrieval service. 5. **Add variety.** A stable exploration bonus is bounded at 0.06. Greedy reranking penalizes repeated topics by 0.07 or 0.17 depending on the experiment variant, and repeated creators by 0.04. 6. **Measure the experience.** Opening a displayed card logs an impression, its features, score and experiment assignment. Playback accumulates only while visible and playing; the server also caps the fraction by elapsed time. Client signals remain untrusted measurements, not verified attention. 7. **Learn within the session.** Feedback immediately updates the interest map; the next retrieved batch uses those interests. Model weights change only through a reviewed training/deployment step. ## Model and evaluation Reproduce the shipped model: ```bash python -m scripts.train_product ``` The synthetic evaluation has 300 query groups of 20 candidates. The first 240 groups train the model and the last 60 groups form the holdout. Query groups do not cross partitions. Time ordering is simulated; these results do not measure real distribution shift. | Metric | FlowRank | Baseline | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Holdout log loss ↓ | 0.4727 | 0.6915, constant training prevalence | | NDCG@10 ↑ | 0.8404 | 0.5140, popularity ordering | | Recall@10 ↑ | 0.7800 | 0.5054, popularity ordering | These are **synthetic benchmark results**, not evidence of improved real-world retention or user satisfaction. See [flowrank/model.json](flowrank/model.json) for weights, bias, split and metric metadata. To experiment with your own opted-in activity exports: ```bash python -m scripts.train_product --exports .local/session-a.json .local/session-b.json --output .local/candidate-model.json ``` This path requires at least 100 explicitly labeled impressions, splits by timestamp and uses feature snapshots captured before feedback. Likes and sufficiently completed watches are positive; explicit skips/hides are negative. Unlabeled exposures are excluded rather than silently treated as negatives. Selection bias remains, and real-data ranking metrics are not fabricated when the exports lack proper candidate-set labels. A small demo catalog/session is insufficient to establish real model quality. Collected visitor data is not automatically used for training. ## API All private routes use the guest cookie. Browser writes require `X-FlowRank: 1` and same-origin requests. Responses are not cached. | Method | Endpoint | Behavior | | --- | --- | --- | | GET | `/health` | Runtime version and database connectivity | | POST / GET | `/api/session` | Start guest session / read current preferences and interests | | GET | `/api/feed?topic=All` | Ranked eligible recommendations | | GET | `/api/catalog` | Search, filter and page through approved reels | | GET | `/api/saves` | Read the current guest’s saved collection | | POST / DELETE | `/api/saves/ID` | Save or remove a reel | | POST | `/api/impressions` | Record a displayed video and return an exposure ID | | POST | `/api/events` | Record owned-exposure watch/like/skip/report feedback | | PATCH | `/api/preferences` | Enable/disable personalization | | GET | `/api/privacy/export` | Export the current session's activity and feature snapshots | | DELETE | `/api/privacy` | Delete session and cascade-delete activity | | GET | `/api/stats` | Current session signal count, catalog count and model metadata | | POST | `/api/admin/catalog` | Admin-only pending metadata ingestion | | PATCH | `/api/admin/catalog/ID` | Admin-only moderation decision | | GET | `/api/maintenance` | Secret-protected scheduled retention cleanup | Example feedback body: ```json {"event_id":"unique-id","impression":"exposure-id-from-server","kind":"watch","watch":0.85} ``` Ownership is checked against the cookie-derived session, not a user ID in the payload. An impression supports one event per kind; retries do not multiply feedback. Admin media imports accept only reviewed assets already packaged with the release. ## Verify and capture product screenshots ```bash python -m unittest discover -s tests -v npm ci npx playwright install chromium # Keep python app.py running in another terminal: npm run test:e2e npm run screenshots ``` Set `BASE_URL` to test a deployed release. The browser suite verifies playback readiness, feedback persistence after reload, insights, opt-out, export, deletion and mobile layout. The optional direct PostgreSQL test uses `DATABASE_TEST_URL`; it is skipped when that variable is absent. The suite creates only disposable random sessions. Six screenshots are saved under `docs/screenshots/`. ## Deployment and operations The app runs on Vercel with durable PostgreSQL in a private schema. See [the operations guide](docs/OPERATIONS.md) for provisioning, secrets, RLS, daily retention, admin ingestion, deployment/promotion, rollback and incident handling. The live demo uses a dedicated FlowRank Supabase project. The repository includes CI tests. Automatic Git-triggered Vercel deployments require the owner to connect GitHub to Vercel; direct CLI deployments are supported independently. Never commit `.env*`, `.local/`, database files, exported user activity or credentials. ## Project structure ```text app.py Product API and production WSGI entrypoint flowrank/store.py SQLite/PostgreSQL transaction adapter flowrank/recommend.py Interests, learned ranking and reranking flowrank/catalog.py Reviewed demo catalog flowrank/model.json Versioned model and evaluation metadata flowrank/engine.py, train.py Original v1 educational baseline static/ Responsive product UI and original playable media migrations/001_product.sql Private schema, database role, indexes and RLS scripts/train_product.py Temporal training and ranking evaluation scripts/generate_media.py Reproducible original motion assets scripts/screenshots.mjs Real product showcase captures tests/ API, training, RLS and browser coverage docs/ Product screenshots and operations guide vercel.json Runtime region and daily maintenance schedule ``` ## Next roadmap - Dedicated database/project, sustained load testing, backup/restore drills, alerting and explicit availability objectives. - Real licensed catalog and upload/transcoding pipeline with object storage, moderation review tooling and abuse controls. - Catalog-scale retrieval and caching, learned multimodal embeddings and a two-tower DL model when data supports it. - Proper randomized item exploration with logged propensities, real temporal validation, fair exposure analysis and statistically powered experiment readouts. - Optional permanent accounts and cross-device identity, carefully designed consent and data portability. ## Video attribution The [catalog manifest](flowrank/real_catalog.json) lists the author, source page and license for each of the 120 distinct files. Video and poster requests go directly to Wikimedia. Availability can change upstream. [Commons reuse guidance](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Commons:Reusing_content_outside_Wikimedia) ## License Code: [MIT](LICENSE). Legacy bundled motion studies: [CC0](static/media/LICENSE.txt).

projects.description: Notebook Lab: interactive Python and R data science learning app with eight lessons, NumPy/pandas examples, a live regression playground, CSV export, progress tracking, and Matplotlib showcases.
projects.readme: # Notebook Lab — ML, Python & R Data Science A personal learning notebook project by **Vamshi Krishna Adam**, covering Python programming, R, numerical computing, data manipulation, visualization, and introductory machine learning. ![Project preview: two Matplotlib line subplots](assets/project-preview.png) *An actual plotting example from the local learning workspace.* ## Project overview This project documents hands-on practice across the Python data science ecosystem and introductory R. The learning materials progress from core collections and object-oriented programming to NumPy arrays, pandas workflows, Matplotlib figures, file handling, SQLite, and regression/classification examples. ## Live interactive demo [**Open Notebook Lab →**](https://python-r-learning-lab-vams2krish.adam-vamshikrishna.chatgpt.site) The hosted demo is **owner-private and requires the owner's ChatGPT sign-in**. This GitHub repository is public, and the app runs locally without login. The runnable companion in [`web/`](web/) includes: - Eight curated Python, R, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, SQLite and ML examples. - Topic filters, text search, empty states and accessible lesson dialogs. - Downloadable `.py` and `.R` examples, with completion progress stored on your device. - Interactive linear regression: adjust slope, noise and sample count; inspect fitted slope, R² and RMSE; export generated data as CSV. - An original Matplotlib plot gallery and responsive layouts. Python/R snippets are read/download examples for local execution. The regression simulator runs in JavaScript in the browser. Generated data is illustrative, and displayed metrics describe training fit. ## Project showcases Actual Chrome screenshots of the local release app. Click an image to inspect it at full size. ### Welcome to the lab ![Notebook Lab homepage](assets/showcase/home.jpg) ### Explore the learning path ![Searchable and filterable lesson catalog](assets/showcase/lessons.jpg) ### Read code and track progress ![NumPy example in an accessible lesson dialog](assets/showcase/lesson.jpg) ### Experiment with regression ![Interactive regression with 60 points and an exact fit](assets/showcase/playground.jpg) ### Original plot gallery ![Matplotlib bar, scatter and histogram examples](assets/showcase/gallery.jpg) ### Mobile experience ## Run the web app locally Requires Node.js 22 or newer. No npm installation or API key is required. ```sh git clone https://github.com/vams2krish/ML-Python-R-Data-Science-Notebooks.git cd ML-Python-R-Data-Science-Notebooks/web npm start ``` Open `http://127.0.0.1:4173`. ```sh npm test ``` The production files are in `web/dist/` and can be hosted by a static web server. `web/server.js` is a loopback development server. Sites deployment metadata is in `web/.openai/hosting.json`; creating a separate Site requires its own Site identity. ## Verification Six automated tests passed. Browser checks covered filtering/search, lesson completion across reload, code and CSV downloads, exact/negative regression fits, reset, gallery images and a mobile viewport. Seven Python examples passed syntax compilation; the collections, objects and SQLite examples ran successfully. Sites confirmed successful deployment. The production sign-in gate was checked, but an authenticated production walkthrough remains unverified because the browser was logged out. See the [verification record](docs/VERIFICATION.md) for results and limits. CI runs the model tests and JavaScript syntax check on pushes and pull requests. ## Repository structure ```text web/ dist/ Static app, lessons, model and plot assets examples/ Downloadable Python and R examples tests/model.test.js Regression and lesson tests server.js Local development server export-examples.mjs Regenerate examples from the lesson catalog assets/showcase/ Six actual browser screenshots docs/VERIFICATION.md Test results and deployment limits .github/workflows/ Continuous integration checks ``` **Original notebook status:** the inventory below describes the local learning collection. The original notebooks, scripts and datasets are not uploaded; the public repo contains the runnable companion, curated examples, selected plot exports and documentation. ## Topics and notebook inventory | Area | Local learning materials | Coverage | | --- | --- | --- | | Python collections | `1.List Tutorial.ipynb`, `2.Dictionary Tutorial.ipynb`, `3.Tuples Tutorial.ipynb`, `4. Sets.ipynb`, `5.Arrays.ipynb` | Accessing, modifying, slicing, iterating, set operations, and practice exercises | | Object-oriented programming | `6.Class & Objects.ipynb`, `7.Inheritance (all types) & super func.ipynb`, `8.Encapsulation Tutorial.ipynb`, `9.Abstraction.ipynb`, `10.Polymorphism Tutorial.ipynb` | Classes, objects, inheritance, `super()`, encapsulation, abstract classes, and polymorphism | | NumPy | `Data.ipynb`, `Numpy/Data.ipynb` | Array indexing, slicing, splitting, copies/views, and linear algebra | | pandas | `Pandas Tutorial.ipynb` | Tabular data practice with pandas and plotting | | Matplotlib | `Matplotlib Tutorial.ipynb`, `3d test.py` | Line plots, customization, subplots, bars, scatter plots, histograms, pie charts, 3D examples, and animation practice | | Files and persistence | `File Handling.ipynb`, `file_handling.ipynb`, `sqlite3.ipynb` | Text and CSV handling, file modes, and SQLite table creation/insertion | | Machine learning | `Sci-Kit Learn Tutorial.ipynb`, `Linear Regression.ipynb`, `Logistic Regression Tutorial.ipynb` | Dataset loading, train/test splits, linear regression, digit classification, and model evaluation | | R | `R_Language/` | Introductory scripts, data import, data-frame inspection, and coursework exercises | The local workspace also contains CSV, Excel, JSON, text, and NumPy data files, plus exported plot images. Selected plot exports appear in the web gallery; the other supporting files remain local. ## Suggested learning sequence 1. Work through the numbered Python collection notebooks. 2. Continue with classes, inheritance, encapsulation, abstraction, and polymorphism. 3. Practice NumPy indexing, array operations, and linear algebra. 4. Explore pandas tabular workflows and file formats. 5. Build and customize Matplotlib charts. 6. Study file handling and SQLite persistence. 7. Move to scikit-learn, linear regression, and logistic regression. 8. Explore the R exercises alongside the Python material. ## Working with the local notebooks These instructions apply when you have the original learning files available locally or after they are added to the repository. ### Python environment Install a compatible Python 3 release and create a virtual environment. From the learning folder on Windows PowerShell: ```powershell python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install jupyterlab numpy pandas matplotlib seaborn scikit-learn openpyxl jupyter lab ``` Open a notebook in JupyterLab and run its cells in order. The package list reflects the main libraries used in the collection; it is not a pinned or tested dependency specification. One list tutorial also imports TensorFlow, which is optional for the core collection exercises and requires its own compatible environment if that cell is used. SQLite, `array`, and `abc` are included in Python's standard library. ### R environment Install R and optionally RStudio. The R scripts use `readr`: ```r install.packages("readr") library(readr) ``` Update local file paths before running the scripts. Some exercises reference external teaching data and may require corrections to paths or object names. ## Practical notes - This is a learning collection with exploratory examples, rather than a packaged application. - Some cells write files or insert database rows; inspect them before rerunning. - Data-dependent examples require their corresponding input files and valid local paths. - Animation export in `3d test.py` requires FFmpeg. - The original notebook suite and its dependency compatibility have not been validated; the web companion has separate tests listed above. - Existing comments and examples may contain mistakes or incomplete exercises; validate behavior as part of practice. ## Learning goals Build confidence with Python fundamentals, understand array and data-frame operations, communicate results with charts, practice basic data persistence, and develop a foundation for statistical computing and machine learning in Python and R. ## Author **Vamshi Krishna Adam** · [GitHub profile](https://github.com/vams2krish) ## License No open-source license has been selected. Public visibility alone does not grant a license to reuse or redistribute the materials.

projects.name: ML-Zoo-Animal-Classification
projects.description: Educational zoo animal classification project using 16 biological traits, K-Nearest Neighbors, exploratory analysis, and a Streamlit prediction app. Includes dataset, training notebook, saved model, setup instructions, and documented evaluation limitations.
projects.readme: # Zoo Atlas · ML Zoo Animal Classification **[Open the live classifier on Vercel](https://ml-zoo-animal-classification.vercel.app)** Zoo Atlas is an interactive field lab for supervised machine learning. Set 16 observable traits or choose an example specimen, then classify it into one of seven animal groups. Each prediction shows the closest reference specimens and the winning share of the weighted vote. ![Zoo Atlas desktop landing page](docs/screenshots/01-desktop-home.jpg) ## Try the product 1. Open **Classifier** and choose an example such as Flamingo or Tuna, or enter a custom set of traits. 2. Select **Classify specimen** to see the predicted group, vote share, and matching records. 3. Change a trait to invalidate the old prediction. **Reset** returns the editor to its initial state. 4. Open **Field notes** for the classification flow, class distribution, and evaluation comparison. 5. Select **?** beside a trait or component for its meaning, examples, and allowed values where applicable. The vote share describes agreement among voting neighbors. It is not a calibrated probability. Example specimens come from the reference data, so their demo predictions are not a measure of generalization. ## Screenshot gallery The screenshots were captured from the running product using Playwright. The wildlife artwork in the hero was AI generated; the interface shown is the actual application. | Bird prediction | Fish prediction | | --- | --- | | ![Flamingo traits and bird classification](docs/screenshots/02-bird-prediction.jpg) | ![Tuna traits and fish classification](docs/screenshots/03-fish-prediction.jpg) | ![Field notes showing animal groups and validation](docs/screenshots/04-field-notes.jpg) | Mobile home | Mobile prediction | | --- | --- | | | | | Leg count help | Weighted vote help | | --- | --- | | ![Leg count help with allowed values](docs/screenshots/07-trait-help.jpg) | ![Weighted vote help showing its range](docs/screenshots/08-weighted-vote-help.jpg) | ## Dataset and model The bundled [UCI Zoo dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/111/zoo) contains 101 records, 16 input features, and seven labels: mammal, bird, reptile, fish, amphibian, insect, and other invertebrate. The legacy CSV matches the official feature and animal-name rows but omits the class label. The current product uses the official class label and treats the animal name as a record identifier. The browser runs weighted K-nearest neighbors with a cutoff of three. A binary mismatch adds one to squared distance; leg-count differences are divided by eight before squaring. All neighbors tied at the cutoff are included. Each gets a vote of one divided by one plus squared distance. Class ties use the nearest contributor, then the numeric class label. One shared implementation handles interactive predictions and evaluation. Grouped leave-one-out evaluation classified **93 of 101 records correctly (92.1%)**, compared with **41 of 101 (40.6%)** for a majority-class baseline. The evaluation excludes every record with the same name as the test specimen, including both frog records. On this dataset, recall was lowest for reptiles (3/5) and other invertebrates (7/10). This is a benchmark on a small reference dataset, not an independent test on new populations or a species identification result. The UCI catalog credits Richard Forsyth and licenses the Zoo dataset under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Dataset DOI: [10.24432/C5R59V](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5R59V). No separate software license has been declared. ## Design system | Token | Color | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | Canvas | #FAF4E8 | Page and input backgrounds | | Surface | #FFFAF1 | Panels and reference cards | | Raised surface | #E7EFE3 | Active trait controls | | Ink | #20372F | Primary text | | Muted ink | #465E51 | Descriptions and secondary labels | | Teal | #176457 | Primary actions, selected states, predictions | | Terracotta | #A3432B | Keyboard focus and section labels | | Border | #A49D87 | Panel and control outlines | The interface uses system typography, grouped native form controls, clear focus rings, and a live region for prediction updates. The two-panel desktop workspace stacks on mobile. The design tokens are defined in [web/style.css](web/style.css). ## Run and test locally Requires Node.js 22 or newer and Python 3 for the local static server. Browser tests use Microsoft Edge. npm ci npm run build python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory dist Open [localhost:8765](http://127.0.0.1:8765). Stop the local server before running the browser suite, which starts its own server on the same port. npm test npm run test:e2e Model tests cover dataset labels, unseen animal names, invalid inputs, distance ties, and benchmark accounting. Browser tests cover initial loading, presets, predicted labels, neighbor explanations, edits, reset, field notes, mobile custom input, and dataset request failure. They also refresh the eight gallery images. [vercel.json](vercel.json) configures the static build and its output directory for deployment. No API keys, backend, or serialized model are needed by the app. - [web](web) — UI, model, and labeled CSV - [tests](tests) — model and product verification - [docs/screenshots](docs/screenshots) — desktop and mobile gallery - [archive/legacy](archive/legacy) — historical Streamlit prototype and original notebook/model; kept for reference

projects.name: network-systems-duetsync
projects.description: Computer Networks / Distributed Systems: DuetSync lets long-distance couples listen together with private rooms, matched local audio, shared playback, clock synchronization, drift correction and reconnect recovery. Live HTTPS/WSS demo, durable Supabase state, browser tests and product screenshots. Not ML or DL.
projects.readme: # Network Systems — DuetSync ### Two places. One moment. [![Verify DuetSync](https://github.com/vams2krish/network-systems-duetsync/actions/workflows/verify.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/vams2krish/network-systems-duetsync/actions/workflows/verify.yml) **[Open the live product →](https://duetsync.vercel.app)** · [Backend health](https://wweuhpqsuwwcbgheckve.supabase.co/functions/v1/duet-sync/healthz) · [Operations guide](docs/OPERATIONS.md) · [Browser verification](docs/browser-verification.json) DuetSync gives long-distance couples a private listening room: invite your person, choose the same song, get ready, and press play together. Shared controls coordinate both playheads while your audio files stay on your own devices. **Project type: Computer Networks / Distributed Systems / Full-stack Web Application.** This is **not ML, DL, or Generative AI**. Playback uses deterministic clock estimation, versioned state and drift correction; there is no trained model, inference, or training dataset. ![DuetSync synchronized listening experience](docs/showcase/05-synchronized-playback.png) ## Try the live demo in a minute 1. Open **[duetsync.vercel.app](https://duetsync.vercel.app)** and click **Create our room**. 2. Click **Copy invite link** and open it on your partner's device, or in a separate browser/private window. Click **Join** there. 3. On **both** devices, click **Try demo song** to load “A Little Closer,” our original 90-second synthesized sample. 4. Each person clicks **I'm ready to listen**. Playback becomes available after the audio fingerprints match and both are ready. 5. Press **Play**. Either person can pause, seek, or skip ten seconds for both. To use your own music, both listeners must select the **exact same audio file**. File hashing happens locally; files are not uploaded. The sample can also be [downloaded here](https://duetsync.vercel.app/demo.wav). ## Product showcase These are actual application screenshots captured during the automated two-listener flow. Test rooms are ended after verification, so any pictured invitation has expired. ### An inviting room for two ![Welcome screen and three-step onboarding](docs/showcase/01-welcome.png) ### Share an invitation, then meet in the music ![Invitation and waiting-for-partner state](docs/showcase/02-invitation.png) ### Catch different recordings before playback ![A mismatched audio fingerprint blocks shared playback](docs/showcase/03-file-matching.png) ### Matching audio, two ready listeners ![Verified audio and both listeners ready](docs/showcase/04-ready-together.png) ### Recover a dropped connection ![Playback pauses while a reserved session reconnects](docs/showcase/06-reconnection.png) ### Made for your phone, too ## What's implemented in v2 | Capability | Product behavior | | --- | --- | | Durable rooms | Shared PostgreSQL state survives worker restarts and is visible across backend instances | | Private invitations | Random 128-bit invitation codes; fragment links keep codes out of ordinary HTTP requests | | Listener sessions | Random 256-bit per-tab session credentials, hashed before storage | | Two reserved seats | Disconnections reserve the listener's seat; another person cannot silently take it | | Room locks | Creator can lock/unlock; rooms automatically lock when both seats are occupied | | File fingerprinting | SHA-256 over the full file plus a duration check prevents different recordings from playing together | | Readiness | Both listeners explicitly unlock browser audio and signal readiness before playback | | Shared transport | Play, pause, seek and skips use server-authoritative, scheduled playback state | | Drift correction | Small drift adjusts playback rate within ±3%; drift over 250 ms triggers a seek | | Recovery | Exponential backoff with jitter, rejoin, state reload, and explicit readiness after reconnect | | Heartbeats | Application health checks, WebSocket ping/pong, presence leases and stalled-connection recovery | | Lifecycle | Creator ends the room; partner may leave; inactive rooms expire after 30 minutes, with a 24-hour hard limit | | Abuse controls | Durable attempt/action quotas, payload limits, bounded queues, slow-consumer limits and origin validation | | Deployment | HTTPS frontend on Vercel, WSS backend on Supabase Edge Functions, private PostgreSQL storage | | Verification | Server integration tests, automated two-browser product flow, mobile checks and CI | ## How synchronization works ```text Listener A ─── WSS ──→ Supabase WebSocket worker A ──┐ local audio ├── PostgreSQL CAS room store Listener B ─── WSS ──→ Supabase WebSocket worker B ──┘ local audio shared room logic Vercel serves the static interface over HTTPS. Workers share durable state; clients never receive database credentials. ``` ### Shared clock Clients send timestamped pings. Given client send time `t0`, client receive time `t1`, and server timestamp `ts`: ```text roundTripTime = t1 - t0 clockOffset = ts - (t0 + t1) / 2 serverNow = clientNow + clockOffset ``` The lowest-round-trip sample supplies the current offset estimate. Clients resample every five seconds and after returning to the foreground. This is an NTP-style estimate that assumes roughly symmetric delays, not a full NTP implementation. ### Scheduled playback A state contains `{ playing, position, at, revision }`. Commands are scheduled **1,200 ms ahead**, leaving time for durable storage and cross-worker delivery. Workers refresh active room snapshots every **400 ms**, with overlapping refreshes suppressed. When a message arrives late, the client computes the expected playhead from its timestamp rather than starting from zero. ```text expectedPosition = position + max(0, serverNow - at) / 1000 // while playing ``` A pause toggle projects the current authoritative playhead to the scheduled pause time, avoiding a backward jump. Seeks use the explicitly requested destination. Every 500 ms, clients measure local drift and either gently adjust playback rate or seek to catch up. These are software targets, **not a guarantee of acoustically simultaneous output**. Network asymmetry, browser scheduling, buffering and audio output hardware all contribute latency. ### Consistency, readiness and recovery PostgreSQL atomically compares the document version before saving a change. Concurrent room mutations retry against fresh state. Playback commands also carry the last observed playback revision, so a delayed control cannot overwrite a newer one. Competing joins cannot claim a third seat. New connections load current state. A session token reclaims the listener's reserved seat; a connection identifier prevents an old socket's close handler from marking its replacement offline. Reconnect pauses the room and clears the reconnecting listener's readiness. The partner waits safely until that listener taps Ready again. Presence leases expire after 20 seconds if a worker dies without a close event. ## Stack and source map | Component | Implementation | | --- | --- | | Interface | Semantic HTML, CSS, browser Audio API and Web Crypto | | Room protocol | Shared JavaScript room protocol used by local Node.js and hosted Edge workers | | WebSocket transport | Native Edge WebSockets; `ws` for the local Node adapter | | Persistence | Supabase PostgreSQL through a service-role-only RPC and compare-and-swap | | Frontend hosting | Vercel production deployment | | Backend hosting | Supabase Edge Functions with platform-provided server credentials | | Testing | Node test runner, Playwright Chromium, GitHub Actions | ```text public/ Interface, playback client and original demo audio lib/app.js Local HTTP / WebSocket adapter lib/hub.js Shared connection protocol, heartbeats and coordination lib/rooms.js Room membership, capabilities and playback rules lib/store.js Development memory store and durable database adapter server.js Local / self-hosted Node entrypoint server.test.js Real WebSocket and concurrency integration tests supabase/functions/duet-sync/ Hosted backend entrypoint and dependency map supabase/migrations/ Ordered schema, service-role access and expiry cleanup scripts/ Static build and original-audio generator test/listening.spec.js Complete two-browser product-flow verification docs/showcase/ Product screenshots .github/workflows/verify.yml Automated test and build checks ``` ## Run locally Requires **Node.js 22+** and npm; CI uses Node.js 24. ```sh npm ci npm start ``` Open `http://localhost:3000`. Local development uses a memory store and the same room logic, without cloud credentials. For a second listener, use another browser/private window; session credentials are scoped to a browser tab. Use a free `PORT` if another app is already running on 3000. ```sh npm test npx playwright install chromium npm run test:e2e npm run build ``` The local browser test starts a dedicated test server on **3187**. To run the same product flow against the live deployment: ```powershell $env:BASE_URL='https://duetsync.vercel.app' npm run test:e2e ``` The build writes `dist/` with the configured public WSS endpoint. `DUET_SOCKET_URL` can override that endpoint during build. Secrets are never included in the static frontend. See the [operations guide](docs/OPERATIONS.md) for deployment, schema and environment instructions. ## Verification and practical limits The [checked-in browser report](docs/browser-verification.json) records the tested URL, sampled playhead drift and completed checks. The browser test uses two independent Chromium contexts and exercises invitations, audio mismatch rejection, readiness, actual media playback, seeking, pause, socket reconnection, reserved-seat recovery, room ending and a 390px mobile viewport. JavaScript page errors must be absent for the test to pass. The verified live run recorded **7.8 ms median** and **29.1 ms maximum** playhead difference across 12 samples, with **zero page errors**. These are results from two independent browser contexts on one machine using the public backend, not a distant-device acoustic benchmark. Seven server integration tests also passed. Server integration tests additionally verify cross-instance state sharing, concurrent seat claims, stale revisions, ownership, expired rooms, origin checks, malformed messages, hidden environment files, payload limits and quotas. The database rejects unauthenticated RPC access. Security advisors report no warnings; private tables intentionally have RLS enabled without public policies. **Scope:** this is a deployed, hardened product demo. It has not been independently security audited, load-tested at scale, or acoustically measured across physically distant devices. No uptime SLA or cross-device audio-latency guarantee is claimed. ## Privacy and operating boundaries - Local audio stays local. The backend stores fingerprints, duration, room membership, readiness and playback state; names of local files are not sent. - Invites are bearer capabilities. Keep them private; the creator can lock the room or end it. This is invitation-based access, not verified personal identity or an account login. - Tokens are kept in `sessionStorage`; losing that storage loses the reserved seat credential. Ending the room and creating a fresh one is the recovery path. - Full-byte hashing requires matching files, including metadata. Different encodings or metadata tags can produce different hashes for the same song. - Audio files are limited to 100 MB and 24 hours; supported formats depend on the browser. File hashing temporarily allocates file-sized memory. - Room and quota tables are private with RLS and no browser policies. A fixed-search-path privileged RPC is callable only by the backend service role. Platform credentials never reach browsers. - Scheduled database cleanup runs every ten minutes. Expiry is enforced on access even before physical cleanup. - Workers have platform lifetime limits, so reconnect support is part of normal operation. Background tabs and sleeping mobile devices may pause or delay playback. - Rooms use periodic snapshot coordination. For large scale, replace frequent reads with shared pub/sub and benchmark storage throughput and cost. - Use only music you have the right to play. No Spotify, Apple Music or other commercial streaming integration is included. ## Next roadmap Completed: matching-file checks, partner readiness, reconnect recovery, stale-socket heartbeats, access-controlled rooms, durable coordination, expiry cleanup, original sample audio, deployment, automated browser verification and the product gallery. Remaining work: physical two-device acoustic benchmarks, Safari/iOS/Android coverage, high-volume load and chaos testing, push-based cross-worker pub/sub, optional account identity, and independently reviewed security controls. These are future capabilities rather than implied features of this release. ## License Application code is [MIT](LICENSE). The generated “A Little Closer” demo audio is dedicated to the public domain under [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/); it contains no third-party recordings or samples. CSS record artwork is original to this project.

projects.readme: # Networking - TogetherPlay **Different places. Same moment.** A synchronized video and audio room for long-distance couples, with durable room recovery, coordinated buffering, and live synchronization telemetry. **[Open the live demo](https://togetherplay-nine.vercel.app)** · [Source code](https://github.com/vams2krish/networking-togetherplay) **Project type:** Computer Networking / Distributed Systems / Full-stack Web Application. This project does **not** use ML, deep learning, or generative AI. Coordination is deterministic; no model, training dataset, inference service, or AI API is required. ## Product showcase Real browser captures of the running product, generated during end-to-end verification. Telemetry readings are individual observations, not synchronization benchmarks. Test room invitations expire after six hours. **Production verified October 29, 2026:** the gallery below was refreshed from the public production URL using isolated Chromium sessions. [Inspect the timestamped test evidence](docs/production-verification.json). ### A shared space, made for two ![TogetherPlay desktop room](docs/showcase/01-desktop-room.png) ### Both people ready before the moment starts Playback waits until every connected participant enables audio and loads enough media. A buffering participant pauses the shared timeline; readiness resumes it. ![Coordinated playback readiness](docs/showcase/02-coordinated-readiness.png) ### Listening together, with live network readings ![Two people playing the same track with synchronization telemetry](docs/showcase/03-playing-together.png) ### Your partner's view Host-only controls are enforced by the server. Partners can enable audio and set local volume; the host may enable shared playback controls. ![Partner view with host permissions enforced](docs/showcase/04-partner-view.png) ### A room that fits your phone ### Video playback ![Shared video playback](docs/showcase/06-video-playback.png) The video showcase uses the flower sample referenced in [MDN's video documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/video). It loads directly from MDN; TogetherPlay does not redistribute that video. The built-in audio track is an original synthesized melody with no third-party samples, reproducible with `npm run demo:generate`. ### A space reserved for two A third independent browser receives an explicit capacity message and cannot enter the room. ![Two-person room capacity enforced in a third browser](docs/showcase/07-room-capacity.png) ## Latest production verification The October 29 run targeted **https://togetherplay-nine.vercel.app**, with the health endpoint confirming PostgreSQL storage. It completed all eleven recorded checks with no uncaught browser JavaScript errors. | Flow | Verified result | | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Room creation and invitation | Creator is host; a separate browser joins as partner. | | Readiness barrier | Host media stays paused until the partner enables audio. | | Actual playback | Audio advances in both browser sessions; external HTTPS video decodes and advances. | | Shared transport | Seeking propagates; pause stops the partner's media element. | | Permissions | Partner playback controls are disabled until the host unlocks them; the partner can then start playback. | | Recovery | Both browsers reload into their existing roles with the same media and room membership. | | Mobile | The 390px layout has no horizontal overflow. | | Capacity | A third independent browser is denied entry. | The [machine-readable evidence](docs/production-verification.json) records the UTC timestamp, target, storage mode, checked behaviors, and one observed playback difference. Both browsers ran on the same test machine over the public HTTPS/WSS service. This verifies the live product flow; it does not establish long-distance timing percentiles, real-phone compatibility, unclean-network recovery, or sustained production load capacity. ## Try it 1. Open **[TogetherPlay](https://togetherplay-nine.vercel.app)** to create a room. 2. Click **Copy invitation** and send it to your partner. Use a separate browser or device for their view. 3. Click **Try the original demo track**, or load an accessible direct HTTPS media URL. 4. Both people click **Enable my audio** to satisfy browser playback permission requirements. 5. The host clicks **Play together**. Pause and seek affect the shared timeline. 6. Uncheck **Host controls playback** to let either participant control playback. No signup is required. Invitations grant guest access to an available seat; keep them private. The host credential stays in that tab's session storage and is excluded from invitations. Reloading preserves it. Clearing session storage or changing browsers loses host privileges; create a new room in that case. ## Roadmap delivered in v2 | Step | Implemented behavior | | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Coordinated buffering | The server pauses while any active member is unready, then resumes requested playback when all are ready. New media invalidates old readiness messages. | | Sync telemetry | Round-trip latency, local drift before correction, connection count, and readiness count. Rounded participant measurements live in transient room state. | | Host permissions | Host-only playback by default. Only the host may change this setting. | | Expiry | Fixed six-hour lifetime; expired rooms cannot be revived. Expired records are cleaned when a new room is created. | | Abuse controls | Two seats; ten creations per IP-derived identity per hour; 1,000 active rooms; per-instance connection caps; message rate limits; 4 KiB payloads; join timeout and bounded backpressure. | | Durable state | PostgreSQL row locks serialize mutations. Shared database state and one-second reconciliation coordinate separate server instances. | | Recovery | Exponential reconnect backoff with jitter, authoritative state reload, readiness re-establishment, and local pause on connection closure. | | Live deployment | HTTPS/WSS on Vercel, verified database TLS, health endpoint, CI, multi-instance database tests, two-browser audio/video verification, and mobile screenshots. | ## Local setup Requires Node.js 22 or newer. CI and deployment use Node.js 24. ```sh npm ci npm start ``` Open `http://localhost:3000`. Development uses process memory when `DATABASE_URL` is absent. Production and Vercel require a database and fail at startup without one. For persistent local rooms, configure a gitignored `.env.local` from `.env.example`, then run: ```sh node --env-file=.env.local server.js ``` For LAN use, both devices open `http://YOUR_LAN_IP:3000` with the same invitation. Clipboard access may require HTTPS; a copy failure displays the invitation as text. A localhost invitation only works on the same computer. ## Architecture and networking ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Host browser] <-->|WSS commands and state| S1[Node instance A] B[Partner browser] <-->|WSS commands and state| S2[Node instance B] S1 <-->|Transactions and row locks| DB[(PostgreSQL)] S2 <-->|Transactions and row locks| DB M[HTTPS media origin] -->|Independent delivery| A M -->|Independent delivery| B ``` - **WebSockets over TCP:** reliable, ordered messages within each connection. Separate connections can reach different instances. - **Authoritative state:** room mutations use short database transactions with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Cross-instance reconciliation runs once per second for active rooms. This uses database polling, not pub/sub. - **Clock estimation:** application ping/pong messages estimate server time using the round-trip midpoint. The lowest-RTT sample among the latest ten determines the offset. This is NTP-inspired, not NTP. - **Drift correction:** every three seconds, clients compare media position to the authoritative timeline and seek if drift exceeds 350 ms. This threshold is a configuration value, not a measured timing guarantee. - **Readiness barrier:** playback requires a source, a requested play state, at least one active member, and readiness from every active member. Solo preview works; joining a second person introduces their readiness requirement. - **Presence leases:** transport pings run every 15 seconds; leases expire after 45 seconds. Clean disconnects pause immediately. Unclean failures can take longer to detect. - **HTTP range requests:** the built-in audio supports byte ranges for seeking. ```text estimatedServerNow = clientNow + estimatedClockOffset playingTarget = savedPosition + max(0, estimatedServerNow - updatedAt) / 1000 pausedTarget = savedPosition ``` Cross-instance propagation, buffering, asymmetric network latency, and device decoding introduce delay. This does not provide sample-accurate audio synchronization. There is no WebRTC, STUN, TURN, or media relay. ## Protocol and security Clients send `create` or `join` with a random 256-bit session capability. The server stores its SHA-256 hash. Creating a room returns a random 128-bit room identifier; joining a missing room never creates one. The creator's hashed capability grants host privileges. Connection identifiers prevent a replaced socket from removing its replacement session. Other messages are `ping`, `source`, `control`, `settings`, `ready`, and `telemetry`; responses are `joined`, `state`, `pong`, and `error`. Playback and readiness commands include a source revision. Snapshots exclude credential hashes, connection identifiers, and raw IPs. ```json { "type": "control", "playing": true, "position": 12.5, "sourceRevision": 1 } ``` Data lives in an isolated `togetherplay` schema in the existing DuetSync Supabase project. It is not exposed through Supabase's Data API. RLS policies restrict application access to a dedicated `togetherplay_backend` database role with grants on only the two application tables. The application does not use a database administrator or Supabase service-role key. Queries are parameterized, pools are bounded, and database TLS verifies the CA and hostname using the public Supabase certificate in `certs/`. HTTP responses include CSP, no-referrer, nosniff, anti-framing, and restrictive camera/microphone/geolocation policies. Selected media must use HTTPS, except the fixed built-in `/demo.wav` asset. Credential-bearing URL userinfo is rejected. Browser WebSocket origins must match the current host, or optional exact `APP_ORIGIN`. Native clients may omit Origin but still require valid room/session capabilities. ## Deployment and operations The demo uses Vercel Fluid Compute and an exported Node.js HTTP server with `ws`; see [Vercel's WebSocket documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/functions/websockets). Durable external state is necessary because separate connections and reconnects may reach different instances. 1. Provision a dedicated database login named `togetherplay_backend` with a securely generated password, no superuser/database-creation/role-creation privileges, a short statement timeout, and database `CONNECT` permission. 2. Apply `db/schema.sql` as an administrator once. It creates only TogetherPlay's schema, tables, indexes, policies, and restricted grants. Never put passwords in this script. 3. Set server-only **Secret** environment variables `DATABASE_URL` and `RATE_LIMIT_SALT` in Vercel. Copy the transaction pooler host from the database's Connect dialog and use the custom database role's username. Never expose these variables to browser code. 4. Link the intended Vercel project and verify the owner and project before deploying. 5. Stage with `vercel deploy --prod --skip-domain`, test the returned URL, then `vercel promote `. 6. Check `GET /healthz` returns `{"status":"ok","storage":"postgres"}` and run the browser suite against the public address. `APP_ORIGIN` optionally pins one accepted browser origin. `RATE_LIMIT_SALT` hashes the IP-derived creation quota identity. The application avoids logging tokens, media URLs, raw IP addresses, and connection strings. Vercel function duration is 300 seconds: clients reconnect on function rotation and reload persistent state. The function runs in `sfo1`, near the database. Self-managed hosts can run `npm start` behind HTTPS with WebSocket upgrades enabled. **Operational boundaries:** this is a deployed, tested demo with production safeguards, not an audited or load-certified commercial service. External uptime alerting, log drains, large-scale load testing, an incident response process, and broad browser/device certification are not configured. The health endpoint is available for monitoring. Cleanup is admission-driven, so expired data may remain until the next room creation. Configure backups and retention requirements before collecting sensitive data. ## Verification ```sh npm test # Include the database integration test: node --env-file=.env.local --test test/server.test.js # Against a running local server: npx playwright install chromium npm run test:e2e ``` Set `BASE_URL` to test a deployment. Optional `LIVE_VIDEO_URL` enables the additional video test/showcase. The standard browser suite uses only the original local audio and needs no external media origin. Browser tests intentionally regenerate screenshots in `docs/showcase/`. Set `PRODUCTION_VERIFY=1` when running against production to require PostgreSQL health and update `docs/production-verification.json`. Ordinary local/CI runs do not replace the recorded production evidence. The suite uses separate host, partner, and capacity-check browser contexts and includes a reload of both participating sessions. Coverage includes timeline math, URL validation, readiness pause/resume, permissions, stale revisions, capacity, expired sessions, foreign Origin rejection, separate-server state propagation, host recovery, actual media advancement, seeking, and mobile overflow. CI installs from the lockfile, audits production dependencies, runs backend tests, and runs Chromium end-to-end tests. ## Source layout ```text api/ws.js Vercel entrypoint server.js Standalone Node entrypoint web-server.js HTTP, upgrades, queues, leases, reconciliation room.js Room state machine and public snapshot projection store.js Development memory and transactional PostgreSQL stores sync.js Timeline calculations and URL validation public/ Player interface

projects.description: Overcall [GenAI] - Social sports predictions with virtual tokens, private match rooms, atomic payouts, and OpenRouter vision with human-confirmed results. Next.js, Expo, Supabase, TypeScript, Tailwind and shadcn-style UI. Includes demo, project images, SQL/RLS, tests and setup docs. GenAI integration; no custom ML/DL training.
projects.readme:
# Overcall [GenAI]

### Make the call. Own the moment.

[Hosted app](https://overcall-genai.vercel.app) · [Live setup and verification](docs/LIVE_SETUP.md)

The current hosted deployment retains Vercel Authentication.

![Overcall project cover](apps/web/public/project-cover.svg)

**Overcall** is a social sports prediction app for small groups of friends. Create spontaneous Yes/No props, stake virtual tokens, talk in the match room, and compete for bragging rights. OpenRouter vision can read a shared scoreboard and suggest a result. **A human confirmation rule always comes before settlement.**

**Project type: GenAI / full-stack application.** It integrates existing multimodal foundation models through OpenRouter. It does not train a custom machine-learning (ML) or deep-learning (DL) model. Its vision provider may internally use deep learning, but this repository is an application/integration project, not an ML/DL training project.

> Virtual tokens only. No deposits, purchases, withdrawals, transfers for money, or cash redemption.

## Product preview

![Match room with live cricket scores and illustrated playbook](docs/showcase-room.jpg)

| Prediction form | Token wallet and ledger |
| --- | --- |
| ![NBA prediction form](docs/showcase-create.jpg) | ![Wallet with payout, reward, and refund entries](docs/showcase-wallet.jpg) |

The interface uses ink and slate surfaces, silver text, and violet accents with an original logo and animated sports illustrations. Web sounds are off by default and can be enabled from the top bar. Motion follows the system reduced-motion preference.

## What's implemented

- **Web match room:** custom props, sports filters, search, personal calls, review queue, token pool shares, chat, group standings, and wallet history.
- **Custom prop rules:** fixed, match-initiator, or chosen stake; timer/manual/event-host locks; permanent entry closure; one entry per user per prop.
- **Human settlement:** majority, initiator plus one, or admin confirmation policies; evidence proposals, accept/reject voting, deterministic proportional payouts, and full void refunds.
- **Virtual economy:** 1,000 starting tokens, 50-token daily reward, immutable client-facing transaction ledger, integer arithmetic, atomic debits/refunds/payouts, and duplicate-entry/payment constraints.
- **Supabase backend:** full schema, indexes, RLS on every application table, signup trigger, guarded RPCs, private evidence bucket, and realtime subscriptions.
- **OpenRouter vision:** authenticated Edge Function, image/JSON validation, configurable multimodal model, per-prop throttling, null-on-uncertainty extraction schema, confidence-gated proposals, and shared room scoreboard capture with periodic frames. Human evidence is an alternative.
- **WebRTC broadcasting:** one host streams a selected scoreboard to up to nine viewers, using authenticated, recipient-only Supabase signaling. TURN credentials are issued server-side when a coturn relay is configured.
- **Groups:** create private rooms, add existing accounts by ID, configurable confirmation and strict-mode settings in the group dialog and via RPC. Strict mode records missed participation rather than automatically expelling friends.
- **Community:** public text feed posting and private follow database primitives.
- **Expo native client:** email magic links with PKCE and optional OTP, private room selection, prop cards, creation, joining, evidence proposals, votes, settlement, daily reward, secure session storage, and realtime refresh. Native vision and full feature parity remain future work.
- **Demo mode:** a clearly labeled local experience without credentials. Demo uses simulated admin confirmation; connected groups default to participant majority.

Live scoreboards cover Cricket, NBA, NFL, MLB, NHL, and Premier League soccer. Cricket uses ESPNcricinfo live-scores RSS by default, with an optional richer CricketData.org adapter. Other sports use ESPN public scoreboards. Source timestamps and stale states are visible. No Odds API is used; pool shares are calculated in-house.

## Stack

| Layer      | Technology                                                               |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Web        | Next.js 16.4.5 App Router, React 19, TypeScript                          |
| UI         | Tailwind CSS 4, local shadcn-style components, Radix Dialog/Slot, Lucide |
| Mobile     | Expo SDK 58, React Native 0.88, SecureStore                              |
| Backend    | Supabase Auth, Postgres, Realtime, Storage, Deno Edge Functions          |
| GenAI      | OpenRouter multimodal Chat Completions with structured outputs           |
| Validation | Zod, TypeScript                                                          |
| Testing    | Node test runner, tsx, PGlite Postgres integration tests                 |
| CI         | GitHub Actions: tests, types, production build                           |

## Run the web app

Requires Node.js 24 and npm.

```bash
npm ci
npm run dev
```

Open [the local preview](http://127.0.0.1:3000). Without credentials, the app starts in demo mode. Demo data persists in browser local storage; Settings & help contains a reset action. No API keys are needed for the demo.

## Connect Supabase

1. Create a Supabase project or start the local Supabase stack with Docker.
2. Copy `.env.example` to `apps/web/.env.local`. Set only `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` there for the web client.
3. Using a working Supabase CLI, link the selected project and apply the migration in `supabase/migrations`. Inspect `supabase db push --dry-run` before applying to any existing database.
4. Enable email sign-in and allow the actual web origin in Auth redirect URLs. For local use, allow both `http://localhost:3000` and `http://127.0.0.1:3000`.
5. Restart Next.js, sign in, create a group, and add friends who have already signed in. The signup trigger provisions each profile and starting grant.
6. Run Supabase security/performance advisors and test policies against real accounts before a production launch.

```bash
supabase login
supabase link --project-ref YOUR_PROJECT_REF
supabase db push --dry-run
supabase db push
```

The migrations are deployed to a dedicated live Overcall Supabase project. Automated PGlite tests cover the same schema, and a live Postgres rollback-only smoke check verified quorum, payouts, RLS, and private signaling. See [live setup and verification boundaries](docs/LIVE_SETUP.md).

## Configure OpenRouter vision

Set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` and `OPENROUTER_VISION_MODEL` in **Supabase Edge Function secrets**. Choose a model that supports both image inputs and JSON-schema structured outputs. No model is hard-coded because availability and provider capabilities vary. Use the dashboard's secret editor; never put provider secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` or `EXPO_PUBLIC_*` variables.

```bash
supabase functions deploy vision --project-ref YOUR_PROJECT_REF
```

The configuration disables the gateway's legacy JWT check; the function itself explicitly verifies the bearer token with Supabase Auth before accessing any prop or calling OpenRouter. This supports modern publishable-key clients.

In a locked prop, select **Collect result evidence**, then share the scoreboard or upload a frame. A selected screen is previewed locally and sampled every 20 seconds while the dialog remains open. The AI may propose a result only when the evidence is sufficient and confidence meets the group's threshold. Humans vote, then a member explicitly settles. Vision is never the final authority.

`OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_VISION_MODEL` are **future placeholders only**. There is no direct OpenAI adapter, fallback, or automatic use of an OpenAI credential. No real provider key is included, and no paid inference was run during development.

## Run Expo

The mobile package is intentionally installed separately to keep web-only setup small.

```bash
npm ci
cd apps/mobile
npm ci
# Copy .env.example to .env and configure the public Supabase fields.
npm start
```

Native sign-in uses `overcall://auth/callback` with PKCE and secure verifier storage. Use a development or standalone native build so the custom scheme is registered. The default Supabase email link works without editing templates; optional OTP entry needs a template that includes the code. The native client shares `packages/core` source with web. Native build signing, simulator/device QA, screen capture, and store submission are not part of this initial release.

## Verify

```bash
npm test
npm run typecheck
npm run build
```

Tests execute the actual SQL migration and cover membership isolation, forbidden balance writes, fixed stake validation, duplicate entries, rollback on overspend, lock enforcement, quorum voting, payouts, refunds, repeated finalization, restricted AI write access, expired timers, and daily reward idempotency. Shared logic tests cover transition guards, deterministic integer payout remainders, one-sided pools, and invalid vision results.

## Repository structure

```text
apps/
  web/                    Next.js app and original visual assets
  mobile/                 Expo native client
packages/core/src/        Shared types, validation, state machine, payout math
supabase/
  migrations/             Schema, RLS, indexes, atomic commands
  functions/vision/       OpenRouter vision adapter
tests/                    Domain and SQL integration tests
docs/                     Architecture, API reference, product screenshot
.github/workflows/        CI verification
```

## Release status and scope

This is a working, tested **MVP foundation**, not an audited production betting service. The web demo runs without external services; connected behavior requires Supabase configuration and vision additionally requires OpenRouter credentials. PGlite validates SQL behavior but does not replace real Supabase service, multi-session race, or device tests.

Still to implement or configure: commercial sports-provider SLAs/licensing, complete standard markets, a deployed TURN relay for restrictive networks, native vision capture, automatic event locks, weekly/activity bonuses, opt-in global standings, full follow/profile UX, presence-based participation tracking, and operational abuse/cost controls. Basic live sports feeds and browser WebRTC broadcasting are implemented. OpenRouter still requires an approved key and usable provider quota.

See [architecture and trust boundaries](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) and [RPC/vision API reference](docs/API.md) for detailed rules and limitations.

See the [feature-by-feature product test report](docs/PRODUCT_TEST_REPORT.md) for all six sports, 49 automated checks, production endpoint results, fixes, and the browser/device flows that remain unverified.

## References

- [Supabase row-level security](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security)
- [OpenRouter image inputs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/multimodal/image-understanding)
- [OpenRouter structured outputs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/structured-outputs)
- [Next.js documentation](https://nextjs.org/docs)
- [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com)

## License

MIT. Original branding and app code are provided in this repository; third-party dependencies retain their respective licenses.

projects.description: A playful personal AI-avatar portfolio for Vamshi Krishna Adam: local Ollama RAG over GitHub projects and READMEs, searchable illustrated gallery, Calendly discovery-call booking, optional AUTOMATIC1111 avatars, and responsive design. Built with Node.js and vanilla JavaScript.
projects.readme:
# PortfolioBot

Vamshi Krishna Adam’s project portfolio, with GitHub-powered project discovery and an assistant grounded in public project documentation.

[Live portfolio on Vercel](https://portfoliobot-nine.vercel.app/) · [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/vams2krish/PortfolioBot) · [Import into Vercel](https://vercel.com/new/clone?repository-url=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fvams2krish%2FPortfolioBot)

![Portfolio homepage](docs/assets/portfolio-hero.png)

| Product view | Screenshot |
| --- | --- |
| Project gallery | [Browse projects](docs/assets/project-showcase.png) |
| Project detail | [Screenshots and deployment links](docs/assets/project-details.png) |
| Project assistant | [Scoped answer with sources](docs/assets/project-avatar-chat.png) |
| Contact | [Booking and contact links](docs/assets/contact.png) |
| Mobile | [Responsive homepage](docs/assets/portrait-mobile.png) |

## Run locally

Requires Node.js 20+. Run `npm start` and open http://127.0.0.1:4175/. Run `npm test` for automated tests and `npm run sync:github` to refresh the project snapshot manually.

Ollama is optional. When available, the local assistant answers using retrieved portfolio context; otherwise it shows relevant excerpts and source links. Configure `OLLAMA_URL` and optionally `OLLAMA_MODEL` in the process environment. The local-only image endpoint uses `AUTOMATIC1111_URL` and saves generated output separately from the supplied headshot.

## Deploy to Vercel

Import this repository using the link above. The project serves static assets from `public/` and API routes from `api/`. Hosted mode uses source excerpts and booking links without connecting to the local Ollama or image server. The hosted catalog reads the published snapshot from GitHub, so scheduled data refreshes also reach the live site.

## Product flows

- Search the catalog by project name, description, category, or tags. Combine category, technology, and public demo filters, then sort by recent activity, featured order, or name.
- Open a project to browse its available screenshots, description, technologies, and links.
- Open the source repository, a hosted demo, or a notebook when available. Owner-only previews and unavailable endpoints are labeled.
- Ask the assistant about a selected project. Follow-up questions stay scoped to that project until the scope is cleared.
- Book a call through Calendly or use the contact links.

## Design and data

The catalog layout and light palette live in `public/catalog.css`. The gallery uses three columns on desktop, two on tablets, and one on phones.

Personal details are in `profile.json`. The GitHub sync collects repository descriptions, languages, topics, READMEs, screenshots referenced in READMEs, and candidates from repository screenshot and documentation folders. It saves up to ten checked image references per project. GitHub Actions maintains the snapshot. Hosted requests cache the current GitHub snapshot for five minutes and use the bundled snapshot as a fallback if the refresh fails.

## API

| Method | Route | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | `/api/profile` | Public profile and project gallery |
| GET | `/api/status` | Local service or hosted mode status |
| POST | `/api/chat` | Question with optional project context |
| POST | `/api/avatar` | Optional local image generation |

Browser checks cover the gallery, search, project details, deployment links, scoped chat, Calendly links, and mobile width. The screenshot gallery shows the application running in hosted fallback mode.
